ployees, and seven the result of compromises and mutual concessions. Two of the strikes in question arose purely out of misunderstandings and were settled by explanations of the real situation.

speechtext: Would the minister please explain the additional expense that this organization will throw upon the country ?

So far as the alteration of the Board of Customs is concerned, It will entail no extra expense-perhaps lessen it. At present the Board of Customs is composed of an officer in Victoria, an officer in Halifax and officers in other outlying ports. The repeal of the existing section and the provision that there shall be a board, the members of which shall be nominated by the Governor in Council, the number of whom can be added to if the necessity arises, will enable us to summon meetings of the board more rapidly and at less expense. With reference to the subsection as to the assistant commissioner, that w-ill add $2,800 to the expense.

is no one in the department who has any feeling about that-none that I am aware of.
The Customs Act is amended by inserting the following section immediately after section 4:-
The Minister of Customs may, from time to time, authorize the employment of such temporary or acting officers of customs in the second or outside division of the Customs Department as are required to carry on the work of the department ; but no such officer so employed shall receive a higher salary than he would be allowed if appointed permanently to the same rank or class ; nor shall any such salary be paid until voted by parliament.

I do not think that section really necessary. It has been the practice of the department since before I came into it to employ men in this way-the department could not be worked otherwise. An officer dies suddenly and his place must be filled. A temporary appointment like this is made. But, when Mr. Newcombe,. the Deputy Minister of Justice was looking over the Act, he thought that possibly it would be well to provide definitely in this way so that there could be no possibility of doubt.

What is meant by saying that ' no such officer so employed shall receive a higher salary than he would be allowed if appointed permanently to the same rank and class ; nor shall any such salary be paid until voted by parliament ? ' As I understand it, there are no classes in the outside service. This, then, compares the position of a temporary appointee with a position that does not exist ? Perhaps the hon. minister will explain.
There are ranks in the outside service-appraisers, chief clerks, clerks, landing waiters, tide waiters, &c.
How would their positions compare with the classes in the inside service ? For instance, does a chief clerk outside rank the same as a chief clerk in the inside service ? Surely not.
No.
How does the hon. minister reconcile that ?

It does not need reconciling. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) will look at the Civil Service Act he will find the ranks or grades of the outside service of the Customs enumerated and a minimum and maximum salary fixed. The exact salary is not fixed, nor do these officers come within the class of those for whom the $50 annual advance is given-the inside service. So, if we appointed a landing waiter temporarily, he could not be paid a higher salary than if he were appointed landing waiter by Order in Council.

Has the minister already power under the law to make these appointments ?
On section 4,
We think so, it has been done for years.
Then, what is the meaning of the clause in the Bill ?

I explained that. There is a revision of the statutes taking place at the present time, and, in looking through the Customs Act the Deputy Minister of Justice, Mr. Newcombe, thought it would be as well that we should have the power stated here expressly. It is absolutely necessary for the working of the department.
I suppose this will be the finishing touch to the Civil Service Act ?
No.
This will give it the coup de grace ?
No, it will not affect it.

The hon. minister, under this, can appoint temporary officers and keep them there as temporary officers at his own pleasure, without it being necessary for them to pass any examination. Will that be the effect of this clause ?
Yes.
Then, what will become of the Civil Service Act ?

Yes ; but they are appointed temporarily. We impress upon them the necessity of qualifying so as to be placed on the permanent staff. They are anxious to get on the permanent staff as soon as they can. For instance, where a collector dies it may be necessary to fill the vacancy at once at that port by some one who has not passed the civil service examination. We have to appoint a collector immediately, and there may be no meeting of the treasury board perhaps for weeks. In these cases we appoint them acting collectors, and as soon as we can we get their medical certificates, and at the first meeting of the treasury board they are made permanent.	.
Then these people need not pass the civil service examination, they may be appointed under the provision of this law ?
Yes.
And they can remain in the service at the pleasure of the minister without passing the civil service examination ?
If then-services are required.
Then practically the Act is done away with.
No more than in the past.

Would it not be better to leave the custom that has prevailed heretofore ? Because if we pass this clause we will admit the principle that temporary officers may be employed contrary to the present law.
No, I would not say that.

Does not the minister interpret that clause as meaning that he may employ temporarily parties who have not submitted to the test of the civil service examination ? I know that has been done, it is being done now; but it would be a mistake to give it the sanction of the law. The minister himself said it was scarcely necessary to pass this law. But if he does pass it, he sanctions a complete departure from the existing law.

No, I would not say that. The Deputy Minister of Justice thinks it would be as well to have the practice put in this express language. It has been the practice of the department from the beginning, and it has been absolutely necessary to follow this practice to carry on the work.

The Minister of Customs said there were a number of so-called temporary officers in the service, some of whom might have been employed as long as twenty years continuously, and the reason they were not put upon the permanent staff of the department is that the time had passed by when they could very well take the civil service examination. There may be some force in his observations with regard to that, but does not this Act put that custom on a permanent basis ?
No.
Will it not have that effect ?
No.

It seems to me it will. Let us assume that we must continue these men who have been for a long time in the service, and who are not on the temporary staff, although to all intents and purposes they are permanent officers. Now, if the minister, in this clause, simply proposes to take power to appoint temporary officers of the department whose employment as such shall continue only for a limited period, it would be a different proposition, from that which is before us. But this provision is wide enough in effect to repeal the whole Civil Service Act so far as the hon. gentleman's department is concerned; because all he has to do is to appoint a man as a temporary officer, and he remains in the department receiving the salary, it may be up to the limit, as if he were a permanent officer. It puts upon a permanent basis that which is now only a custom, and is continued for

tlie reasons of expediency and necessity which the hon. gentleman mentions. If the provision were limited to the appointment for six months, or for such a period as would be reasonable, I could understand it; but I cannot understand the necessity of a provision having so wide a scope as til at which is presented to the House now.

There are cases where we have to appoint them temporarily for the summer, when there may be a press of work. But there will not be the same danger that the hon. gentleman apprehends. Under the present law we can appoint any one in the place of a preventive officer and make him permanent at once; and the minimum and maximum figures that are fixed for the salaries would allow a very wide range. So there is no more danger than before, the department is getting at once more power than it has already, because we could appoint them permanently at once as preventive officers. But we do not wish to do^ that. We have to appoint them temporary at first, and then we urge upon them to pass the examination. But as I said, there is no more danger of wiping out tire Civil Service Act in doing this than under the present law, because all we would have to do would be to appoint them under that clause regarding the appointment of preventive officers and assign them to any duties we liked.

After over fourteen years' experience as collector of customs in the port of Halifax, I may say that I do not know of a single instance where an officer in the outside service was required to pass the civil service examination. The outside service generally consists of landing waiters, tide waiters, lockers, &c., and they are appointed just because they are smart, active people. I do not think the service will be improved by compelling these people to pass the civil service examination. I know that all the time I was in the custom house the outside service were not required to pass the examination. There was no such a thing as a chief clerk, or a clerk at all. wanted for the outside service duties, because they brought their returns into the custom house, and records were kept in the custom house by the officers who were required to keep those records themselves. I think you will find that this is the practice in all the large ports.

The other evening we brought this same question before the hon. gentleman. I am rather surprised that lie does not propose in this Bill to make the temporary officers permanent, clean up the sheet entirely, and see if this grievance cannot be remedied once for all. I mentioned the city of Windsor the other evening, where I find there have been ten preventive officers appointed since the hon. gentleman took hold of the department. There had been men appointed there as preventive officers Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
years before that, and they are still on the temporary list, and I suppose all the new appointments are made permanent. That is what we complain of on this side of the House, that political influence is brought to bear, and men are put on the permanent list who are not entitled to be put on over men who have already been long in the service. If the hon. gentleman put these men on irrespective of their party politics, then perhaps there would not be so much cause for complaint.

I shall lie glad to have them all pass the examination, and in some cases they have passed, while in others they have not. But the hon. gentleman must not think that I am guided by political influence in making these appointments. There have been at least as many Conservatives put on the permanent list of preventive officers as there were under the old government. There were as many Conservatives put on the permanent list as there were others, or at least, as many as had been appointed by the old government.
There are some Conservatives left.
So that it would not be right to make recriminations in that way.

I know of cases of men there who are not on the permanent list and they are as good officers as ever were stationed at Windsor. There are no complaints against them. This is growing to be a very serious complaint, and it will take up the time of the House session after session unless the grievance is remedied. I could see no injustice if there was something in the shape of an Act giving the hon. Minister of Customs power to put these men on the permanent list. Here is an opportunity now, and we could insert an amendment providing for that in the Bill now before the committee.

May I suggest to the hon. minister that if it is the intention of the minister, in making these temporary appointments, simply to place these persons in a training school to prepare them for making an attempt to pass the civil service examination, he might do this by saying that such appointments made after this date shall only hold good for a limited length of time, say six months, and if they are not then able to pass the civil service examination their services will be dispensed with.

I think that is a very wise suggestion of the hon. member for East Sim-coe (Mr. Bennett). There is no doubt that under this clause the hon. minister can employ an officer who is not qualified and keep him employed. That is the intention. It is bad enough that the custom lias prevailed in the past. I do not think we should give 1 the sanction of law to it, and the way to

guard against that is to carry out the suggestion that has been made and which I have incorporated in the amendment which I am now about to read : ' Provided such temporary employment be not continued for a period of more than six months.' This would permit employees to qualify under the Civil Service Act, and would prevent such abuses as those which we know are occurring. I move to add to the section the provision that temporary employment should only last for six months. .

The objection to that amendment would be that if you employed a person temporarily during the busy season of the year and you required to do the same perhaps next year, the person who had had so many months' training would be the very person the collector would want to put his hand on to continue the service for another year.
Could he not qualify in the meantime ?

My experience lias been that in the outside service the qualification required in the inside service is not necessary, and it has not been the practice to ask for the examination of a man in the outside service. These men are in a good many ways more like labouring men with a good education than clerks who would suit in the inside service.
In that case I think it would be better to amend the Civil Service Act directly, and not do it in this way.

Yes. I think that would be a better way than by pressing this amendment if it is considered desirable. In regard to what the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) says, I do not think we could make such an amendment to this Bill. The proposed amendment is one that could be introduced any year, but there would have to be a consultation, and the government would have to be agreed upon it. It is a subject that is on my mind, but I cannot deal with it this year. The suggestion as to six months employment, of course, will not work, because there is only a qualifying examination once a year. There might be an officer appointed very shortly after the examination that takes place this fall, and it would be a year before the board met again, so that six months would not do. If any time at all were fixed, it would have to be a year.
Make it a year.

Would it be fair to make a provision of that kind now ? I think there would be something like a moral obligation to put all officers on the same plane, and we would have to put away all the temporary officers we now have who have been employed for fifteen or twenty years, and who know their business just as well as any officers in the inside service.
It would not accomplish anything if there was any fear that the department would be worked in an impi-oper or unfair way. If there was any danger that political influence might be brought to bear on the minister and he might not hold the scales evenly, you do not obviate it by that, because, as long as there is that provision. I could appoint a temporary clerk and if he could not pass the examination at the end of six months, if I wanted to retain hiip, I could simply appoint him permanently as a preventive officer.
The department has power to do wrong, any way.

It has the power. I do not think the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) will find that there has been any consistent course pursued of ignoring men because of the difference in their position, and I am sure there has not been in the cases he has mentioned. I could give scores of cases where men appointed long before I came into office have been put upon the permanent list.

I think I can fairly complain in these cases I have quoted, because I know some of these men very well, passing up and down there very frequently, as I do. Of course, this side may change to the other, as I am confident it is going to soon, and the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite would be in the same position then as our friends are now. It is hard to explain why men who have been in the service ten or twelve years at least are overlooked, while those who have only been in a few years are made permanent.

I think there is no doubt that the hon. minister is right when he says that he could evade the law, any way; but I do not think that is an argument for us to change the law, because that is what we are doing in this section. In the amendment which I presented I intended to provide for the future only. I have no objection to stating that any amendment with that new disposition will apply to the future, but I think it does that without any such expression. I am quite willing to change the period of six months to a period of one year, but I think it is very desirable that we should not by this subsection change the general trend of the law in regard to qualification for the civil service. What the hon. member for Victoria, N.S. (Hon. Mr. Ross), said may be quite true also. It may be true that in the outside service examination and qualification are not necessary, but it is in the law, and I think we should leave it there.

I think if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) would inquire at the port of Montreal, or Toronto, or St. John, or Halifax, he would not find a single instance where a preventive officer has passed the examination, or was requir-

ed to do so. The education of these men might be more practical perhaps than that of a good many whose education is designed to enable them to pass the civil service examination. The men in the outside service are more like workingmen. A locker receives casks into his warehouse, and he sees they are properly placed and delivered on warrant from the custom-house. These men do not require to pass an examination, and the chances are they would not be as good as they are if they did.
I believe the hon. gentleman is quite right in a good deal of what he says, but is it not the proper course to amend the Civil Service Act so that these gentlemen might be properly appointed.
That is just what I want. I want to get them the increase of salary and promotion they would be entitled to if they did pass the examination.
This amendment does not accomplish that, and under it the minister can appoint any number of temporary clerks to remain there during his pleasure.

If the position of surveyor of customs should become vacant, under this Act the minister could appoint an acting surveyor who had not passed the examination, and he could draw his salary and fill the position during the pleasure of the minister. Would not that make him virtually a permanent employee ? Suppose in the town of Prescott the position of chief clerk were to be vacant, and no doubt there would be a great number of applicants for it, perhaps the government might wish to appoint some one who did not pass the examination and they would appoint him as acting chief clerk. If be filled that position for a number of years he would virtually hold it permanently, although he was not appointed by Order in Council.

Until an officer has been appointed on the recommendation of the treasury board and sanctioned by the Governor in Council he does not become a permanent employee. He might be acting landing waiter and be paid, but he could not be appointed permanently to that rank until he bad passed his examination. and he would lose his time if he were ill and would not be entitled to holidays and so on.

We have a vacancy in the town of Prescott in the Inland Revenue Department which has existed for some time, and if the Minister of Inland Revenue were to introduce such a Bill as this he could appoint a person who had not passed the civil service examination. and the Minister of Inland Revenue knows that there is pressure brought upon him to do that now. Suppose lie should appoint a man as acting inland revenue collector and he remained in office for some years, he would be recognized by the public Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria)..
at least as a permanent officer, and in the case of a change of government or a change of minister even, it would be unfair to dismiss an officer of that kind. I think myself that a person should be appointed to such a position only until such time as he would have an opportunity of passing the civil service examination, and if he failed at first he might be credited with his percentage or something of that kind, but at all events there should be some limit. The public now believe that it is impossible for a minister to appoint a person to a vacancy until he has passed the examination and for that reason the minister is saved a great deal of trouble. If you pass such legislation as this there is no doubt that your staff will deteriorate in time.

In reply to the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr Monk) I wish to say that this is no evasion of the law at all. The law at present provides that inspectors, collectors and preventive officers in the Customs Department may be appointed without examination and without reference to the rules for promotion prescribed. All that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) would accomplish by his motion would be that if a person were appointed, and at the end of the year he would not bo able to pass the civil service examination, he would be dismissed. The civil service examination is largely clerical and I venture to say it would trouble the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) and myself to pass it now. I dare say we could pass it when we left school, and although I do not want to say anything against laws that are in vogue, yet when you come to a practical department like customs, the qualifying examination, in my judgment, is of very little avail. You want general knowledge, you want good judgment and in some cases you want a knowledge of the methods of trade. If a man proves himself to be a good officer, but could not pass the examination, we could then appoint him a preventive officer under the law. But 'wherever we can get them to pass the examination instead of appointing them preventive officers and saying: You discharge the duties of landing waiter, if he does pass the examination his title would be landing waiter or tide waiter or clerk or whatever he is. This makes the practice a little more regular, but there is no change.
Is not that exemption in the civil service law wide enough now ?

This does not make it any wider, but this permits the appointment of an officer temporarily. In some cases these appointments must be done in an emergency and sometimes you cannot summon a meeting of the Treasury Board and get His Excellency's assent in a day or two. There are times when, after a long session of parliament perhaps, some ministers are taking a well-deserved rest for a day or two, and you

might not be able to get a meeting of the Treasury Board or of Council; or His Excellency might be away ; and a month might elapse without anything being done. You must have persons to attend to these duties, and so you appoint them temporarily. The object of the Bill is not to discharge men from the service or get more men into the service without reference to the Civil Service Act. It is simply the result of a suggestion from the Department of Justice that it would be better to have this additional provision that when a person is temporarily appointed to a certain office he shall not receive a larger salary than is paid to a permanent officer of the same rank or class.
Has that been the practice ?
No. In the case of preventive officers there is no limit at all.

The hon. minister knows that it is not customary to appoint a temporary officer to one of the high positions in the service, such as surveyor of customs ; and he would not appoint a man as a preventive officer, and then assign to him the duties of a surveyor. If he has done so, I think he has not rightly understood the law. Under the proposed provision. the minister could appoint any person to the position of acting surveyor, and virtually make him permanent. I understand the minister to take the position that he could appoint any person as a preventive officer, and then allow him to fill the position of chief clerk or surveyor of customs in the city of Toronto.

Yes, he could, but the appointee could not be styled chief clerk ; he would be acting clerk. A great many men who have been appointed preventive officers are taking entries, and are as efficient officers as we have. I think that I have shown that this is a proper provision, and it would be better for the hon. gentleman to withdraw the amendment.

I do not understand liow the hon. minister can say that this Bill which he asks us to pass makes no change. He stated, when we first took up this section, that it was almost unnecessary to pass it; and yet the fact is, if I am not mistaken, that the question having been referred to the Department of Justice, Mr. Newcombe, of that department, stated that the system at present was irregular, that the law was not being observed, and that it would be necessary to pass this amendment in order to regularize the position of these employees. I do not think there is any doubt that under this provision, if we pass it, the Minister of Customs may name a temporary officer, and employ him from year to year temporarily, without subjecting him to what the law requires-the qualifying test of a civil service examination. We had under discussion a day or two ago the estimates of the lion. Minister of Customs, which we now pass eu bloc. The evening before last we voted $129,000 for five or six branches of the Customs Department, and having had the money voted in that general way, the minister can keep a temporary employee continuously in his service without our knowing anything about it. We shall not even go through the form of voting his salary every year notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act. I do not say that the deputy minister of Justice was not right in making that suggestion to regularize the position of those employees ; but the object we ought to have in view is to improve our civil service, not to spoil it, as we have been doing for many years past by this custom. The hon. gentleman knows how in 1896 a very large number of civil servants were dismissed without any opportunity of being heard. I will not go back upon that; it was fully ventilated at the time ; but in my own aounty the number of civil servants who were dismissed without notice and without any opportunity of defending themselves was very great, and much hardship was incurred. Here we are at present still further mutilating our civil service organization. We are doing the exact opposite of what they have been doing in years past in the United States, where they had a deplorable civil service. Under the Cleveland administration a set of men undertook to improve conditions, and at the present moment for over five thousand employees of the government of the United States, there is no more trouble with the spoils system, and they cannot be dismissed. The United States are improving their civil service. England has a much better system of patronage and civil service than we have in Canada, and here we are opening the door to abuse. It has been said on this side of the House, and I think it is worthy of the consideration of lion, gentlemen opposite, that they are preparing trouble for themselves. We know how members belonging to the ministerial party are bothered with demands for employment. Under this section, if we pass it, there would be far greater demands, and members will not have the defence of saying that those who solicit employment will have to pass an examination, because under this proposed section they may be employed temporarily, so to speak, for ever. Under these circumstances, I think we ought not to give the sanction of the law to the unfortunate custom which has prevailed in all the departments in the past, and I think the amendment that has been suggested would be a protection not only to the public, but for hon. gentlemen opposite themselves, and particularly for those in charge of the government departments. We might modify it in the direction suggested by the hon. member for Grenville, so as to provide that

temporary employment will not last beyond the period fixed for the next civil service examination, and that this section will not apply except in the future, if that is necessary. I think all our efforts ought to tend to the improvement of our civil service, and not to its deterioration, and I think the hon. minister, on reflection, will himself acknowledge that we are readily helping him by this suggested amendment.

I do not think the suggested amendment in any way adds to the appeal of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. I think, on the contrary, that the amendment has for its object to cause some of the abuses that have existed for the last twenty years to disappear. My hon. friend is aware that under the Civil Service Act, provision is made for the appointment of officials to the civil service, first, after examination, and, second, on a special report of the deputy head of the department to the effect that the person has special qualifications. In addition to these two modes of appointment, we have, in subsection 2 of section 37, a provision that Customs inspectors, collectors and preventive officers may be appointed without examination and without any reference to the rules of promotion That is to say, you can appoint preventive officers without any reference whatever either to examination or to promotion. But there is no provision in the law defining the duties of a preventive officer. and the practice has grown up in the last twenty years of assigning preventive officers to the performance of special duties. The authority to do this is to be found in section 5 of the Act, which provides that the Customs Department shall have the control and management of the collection of customs duties and matters incident thereto. The result has been that preventive officers have been assigned to the discharge of duties, such as those mentioned in schedule B. for which the regularly appointed officials are paid a different salary. Take, for instance, the case of a clerk. Under the Act he would be only entitled to receive $400 per year, but the duties of clerk may be assigned to a preventive officer who will receive a much larger salary. This anomaly has suggested the amendment which authorizes the appointment of a temporary or acting clerk to perform the duties of a regular clerk, which are now assigned to a preventive officer. We wish to do away with the anomaly that exists at present, and if a temporary clerk is appointed, under this amendment he will not receive any larger salary than the regular official would who is appointed under section 50 of the Civil Service Act. It is for the House to say whether or not it is wise to amend the law which has been in existence all these years, giving authority to the Customs Department to appoint these officials without examination. If the law should be amended, if all these appointments Mr. MONK.
made in the past should be declared irregular, what will become of the service ? The proper thing is to get the sanction of this parliament to do what has been done in the past.
Is there any provision now in the Civil Service Act obliging these men who are appointed temporarily, to pass an examination in a certain period ?
Not preventive officers unless they want to come into the permanent service.
They would remain on permanently although only temporarily appointed ?
Yes.

Then is not the suggestion of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier right that the trend of this legislation is to deteriorate the public service ? The hon. gentleman admits that one-quarter of the outside employees have never passed the examination.

The principle of the clauses is this. Inspectors and collectors were not required to pass a qualifying examination, just the same as post office inspectors and postmasters, and for this reason, in order to be able to give such appointments to parties whose long political service was entitled to some recognition. Any person may be appointed to a department with special qualifications. Suppose the head of the department wants a chemist for analytical purposes, it would be absurd to require such a man to pass the civil service examination. Take a landing waiter, there is no necessity for his passing the civil service examination. But the Act never contemplated that such an officer could be transferred to the position of a clerk without passing the examination. It may be said that that has been done, but it has been done with the understanding that these parties would pass the civil service examination within the year or go back to their old positions. This amendment will justify these appointments in voidance of the Civil Service Act. There is no necessity at all for it. There are thousands of young men in the country, with all the qualifications necessary for any of these appointments, and who have passed the qualifying examinations, but because a person happens to be appointed a landing waiter, he is open, under this clause, to receive any appointment at all in the service.
As I understand the hon. Minister of Justice, he can, under the law, appoint anybody as preventive officer and then promote him to any other position without his passing the examination.

Under the Civil Service Act a man may be appointed without examination, a preventive officer. The law makes no provision for
4C25

the duties to be performed by a preventive | officer, so that the Minister of Customs can assign that preventive officer to any duties he thinks proper, and the practice has been in the past to assign them to certain duties.
What are they ?

Some clerks, some lockers and all manner of duties. A great number of them are in the department, and this is to prevent that practice in the future, by providing that if a preventive officer is assigned to perform the duties of clerk he shall not receive a larger salary than would be paid a clerk regularly appointed.

My point is this : According to law, a person to be appointed a surveyor of customs must have a certain qualification. If you are going to appoint him permanently he must have passed the civil service examination. According to the law, section ten of the Civil Service Act :-
All appointments to the Civil Service shall be during pleasure, and no officer shall be appointed or promoted to any place below that of deputy head unless he has passed the requisite examination and served the probationary term heretofore mentioned.
If you have a preventive officer appointed temporarily you cannot legally transfer him to perform the duties of a surveyor until he has passed the examination. If the law will not allow you to put on an acting surveyor because he has not qualifications, how will it justify you in putting in another officer who has not the qualifications ?
It is possible that the law may have been violated ever since 1886. But, if it has, we desire to remedy that and prevent it occurring in the future.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: With reference to the case mentioned by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) I may say that Mr. Gerald was superannuated and another gentleman appointed in his place who had not passed the examination. He was appointed a preventive officer. He had to take that minor position. The Minister of Customs knows that the gentleman appointed to fill the vacancy caused by the superannuation of Mr. Gerald had been looking for a much higher position for several years, but not having passed the examination, could not be appointed. According to this law, he could have been appointed to one of the higher positions, say as acting surveyor. Now, suppose that were done. If a change of government should take place, I do not hesitate to say I would do all I could to have all appointees under this administration retain their positions, if they had been appointed honourably-that is that they had not been appointed through the unfair dismissal of a supporter of the Conservative party, which, I must say, has not been done so far, and I am not finding fault in that way. If this gentleman were appointed chief clerk or acting surveyor. I would feel in duty bound to recognize the appointment as a permanent appointment. So, what I feel is that the minister is only going to give more trouble to himself and also make a great deal of feeling should a change of government take place.

The surveyor ranks next to the collector in authority in every customs house, because he has control of the outside service, though he is not regarded as a deputy according to the Civil Service Act, I think you will not find a case in any port of Canada where the surveyor has been compelled to pass the civil service examination.
To whom does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid) allude when he speaks of the surveyor ?

There always has been a surveyor until a short time ago, When the position of surveyor became vacant, the hon. gentleman established a chief clerkship instead. The hon. minister knows the gentleman who got the position is qualified. But there may be others who have not the necessary qualifications and could not receive the appointment, but who are recommended by the Liberal committee. Of course, not having passed the civil service examination, they could not be appointed under the law as it is. The person appointed is a first-class man-could not be better fitted for the position. i\ But he had

passed the civil service examination. The hon. minister knows that if this law had not been in force be would not have made the appointment he did, for influence would have been brought to bear upon him to appoint one of the applicants. But, I think that this clause will be unfair to those who have passed the civil service examination. A man can be appointed acting clerk, and so there will be no use in his passing the examination.

The effect of this section has been stated better than I could state it by the Minister of Justice. This amendment to the law will limit and circumscribe the powers that the department now has under the Civil Service Act.
No.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It was limited before.

A preventive officer can be assigned to the duty of a clerk, the maximum salary of whose position would be $1,000 or $1,200 a year, and he could be paid $1,500 or $1,800 if the department thought fit. We do not do that, but it could be done under the law. If this section passes, that will be contrary to the law. Therefore, I say, the power of the department is circumscribed by this section. Now the argument of the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) was that it was not intended that preventive officers should be appointed and thus escape the necessity of passing the examination- they should pass it within a year, for, he says, if they do not pass it within a year, that is evidence that they are unfit for their positions. If the hon. gentleman will say that all temporary officers must pass the examination within a year or leave their positions, then, he will put out some three or four hundred men, some of whom have been in the service for ten, twelve, or fifteen years. They will all have to go. There would be no fairness in drawing the line if, because a man who is appointed now cannot pass the civil service examination at the end of the year, that is proof that he is unfit to discharge the duty; that reason must equally apply to the men who have been there ten or fifteen years. You cannot draw the distinction. If the purpose be to secure efficiency it must apply to all that are in that position. I *do not know that we need to be careful about this clause. If you strike it out you are leaving more power in the hands of the department than it has at present.

I do not think the hon. gentleman is very logical in his conclusions. It has been suggested by my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) that after the temporary officer has occupied the position for a certain time, if lie has not then passed the examination, he should cease to Mr. REID (Grenville).
hold the position. That seems to be reasonable, and I think it is feasible. Perhaps it might be for a longer time than was suggested ; instead of six months the period might be made a year, when certainly it would be time for him to pass his examination. I think the minister could meet the difficulty by providing that a temporary officer should not occupy the position longer than six months, or at all events until the next examination. Now', with reference to the other part, which I think is really of more importance, it is argued that it would be unfair to those who have been in the position for several years as temporary officials. I do not think we should be guilty of any unfairness on this account. We have in this country recognized that vested rights must be respected, and it would be a serious injustice, one of which the opposition would never be guilty at all events, and of which I hope the government would never be the perpetrators. It would be unjust to say that after a man had been in that position for ten or fifteen years, he should now by reason of a new law, be subjected to an examination. We can prescribe that the period during which a temporary employee should occupy that position shall not exceed a certain number of months from the next examination, and that the rights of those gentlemen who have served well and faithfully, and growm old in the service, shall be protected.
The hon. gentleman says ' have served well and faithfully.' But to accept an amendment of this kind is to say that one who does not pass an examination cannot serve well and faithfully.

It would be a hardship for the men who have been in the service fifteen or twenty years and w'ho are not competent to pass an examination, to make it apply to them. But the case would be different with applicants for employment.

This clause is for the purpose of restricting the scope of the Act as it has been construed in the past, because it is alleged to have operated to the detriment of the service. It would only be fair, if this amendment should pass, to make it apply to all those who are in the service as well as to those who are to be appointed. Why draw a line of demarcation between those who came in under an improper construction of the Civil Service Act and those who are brought in now ? Is there not a reason for the rule that has existed for the last twenty years ? I do not say the rule has been improperly established, on the contrary. I think it was properly established, and it has worked out well in results. I will show how it works out well. Take, for instance, a man appointed as an appraiser in the customs. That man requires to have had some actual experience of

business, and if he has been in the business for ten, fifteen or twenty years, lie has some value as an appraiser. But how many of these men who have been in the business during all these years are competent to pass an examination ? How many of them could pass ? How many of them would be disqualified simply because they could not pass Men perform the duties of an appraiser better if they come in after those years of service than if they had simply got that book knowledge which ,is required to pass the examination. It seems to me the rule that has been established by my hon. friend is a rule that operates usefully. But it is better to make the rule clear, to make is absolutely apparent to parliament what we are doing. I think it is better to restrict the Act and prevent what has been done in the past from being done in the future.

The Minister of Justice complains of abuses under the late administration. He will have an opportunity of making a comparison of the defects which existed at the beginning of the hon. gentleman's career and those which exist at the present time. The Minister of Customs has promised to bring down a statement of the number of the employees of the customs in Toronto, which will include a list of those who have been temporarily appointed during the last five or six years, and he will be shocked to learn what numbers of men have been appointed there temporarily, and have been there for years, without passing the examination at all. They are there in utter disregard of the requirements as regards qualifications and age. We heard the statement made the other night that one-fourth of the total number of the officers have never passed an examination at all. We say that if this Bill is passed it will open the door and there will be a larger percentage twelve months from now who have not passed the civil service examination than there is to-day.
Do I understand the hon. minister to approve of the practice whicli has been in existence for twenty years of violating the Civil Service Act and that we should continue it ?

There is not a technical violation of the Act. The Act provides for the appointment of preventive officers without regard to the civil service examination. You can take any man whom you choose .and appoint him a preventive officer in the outside service. There is no Act in existence that I am aware of which defines the duty of a preventive officer. The practice in the department has been, as I am informed-of course I speak subject to correction-when a preventive officer has been appointed to assign him to the performance of these duties under schedule (b). The result has been that at times a man has been appointed as a preventive officer with a fixed salary and he
has been appointed to the performance of the duty of a clerk and while in the performance of this duty without being regularly appointed under the Civil Service Act, he has been appointed at a salary larger as a preventive officer than it would be possible to give him if he were regularly appointed under the Civil Service Act. My object in suggesting the amendment is to do with parliamentary authority what has been done in the past, to make it possible for the Minister of Customs to give temporary employment to a man instead of appointing him a preventive officer, assigning his duties at the time he is appointed, and thus provide that a temporary clerk shall not be in receipt of a sum in excess of the sum to which he would be entitled if he were appointed permanently. I think the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) misunderstood me. What I meant to say was that if these are abuses the abuses originated before 1896, and they have been carried on to the present day. We are all responsible for them. I do not mean to apportion the responsibility. I mean to say that if these abuses are in existence we inherited them and we want to see how far we can restrict them.
There is no improvement up to the present time on the old order of things.
Perhaps only in the character of the individuals appointed.

There are many men in the service temporarily who are good officers and. the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) thinks that they should be put on the permanent list. I agree with him and I might put them on as preventive officers. While the law gives me that power I try not to do that because I have invariably asked them to pass the civil service examination. If they do not pass it. in cases where I have felt that they were good officers, then. I have availed myself of that power. He suggested that there ought to be an Act passed whereby all in the service in that position should be placed on the permanent list. I do not hesitate to say that my own personal view is-I do not commit the government-that it would be a desirable thing to do, but the hon. gentleman will see that if I were to become a party to that, then. I would become a party to making a declaration that my firm belief was that His Majesty's service in the customs could be well and faithfully performed by men who had not passed the civil service examination. I would be recreant to my duty if I came down and proposed that we continue to take into the service of His Majesty men unfitted for it. But, according to the rule laid down by hon. gentlemen opposite, the very fact that these men have not passed the civil service examination is a declaration that they are unfitted for the service. I do not accept that. If I believed that I could not ex-

press my own individual view in favour of doing this by a specific Act and placing them all upon the permanent list. It is to be applied to men who cannot pass and if the fact that they cannot pass the examination is proof that they are unfit to hold positions in the service of His Majesty is it proof that the men who have been employed ten or fifteen years are unfit to serve His Majesty ? I do not believe it. It might be suggested that I am arguing against the Civil Service Act. Well, I am not careful to say that I am a great admirer of the Act in so far as practical benefits are concerned in the working of the outside service of the customs. I do not think it is an advantage. We cannot work the outside service without temporary officers. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not say that I should not avail myself of the services of such officers, but they say that they must pass the examination within a year. I would like to get them to pass it if they are equal in other respects. I would like them to pass before I appoint them at all, but my experience as a business man extending over a good many years, is that you may find a person who would have the literary attainments perhaps, or the knowledge. to pass this examination which is a literary one in relation to matters of geography and history of this country and other countries, that you might find n young man who has passed that, but when it came down to the discharge of the duties of an appraiser, or a clerk, or a landing waiter, where judgment has to be exercised, lie might not be the best officer by any manner of means. If you want to continue your Civil Service Act and apply it to your inside service where your work is largely clerical, all right. I am speaking of the outside department of the customs, and I do not believe that you are going to secure a better class of men if they do pass the civil service examination. So long as this is the law I endeavour to get all I can to pass it, but where I find men-

How have you been succeeding in Toronto in getting men to pass the examination who have been employed during the last five years ? Have yon made very much progress in getting these men to pass the examination ?
Yes, I think so.
How many have passed during the last twelve months ?
I will find out. I do not think many of the old appointments have passed, but I think some who have been appointed ginee I have had charge of the department myself have passed.
You are still urging them to pass ?

We are urging them to pass. The men themselves Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
are very anxious to be put on the permanent list for the reason that if they are on the temporary list and they lose a day through sickness, they lose their pay and they do not get their holiday. More than that, where a man is on the temporary list his services can be dispensed with by a letter from the minister. If he is on the permanent list an Order in Council must be passed to dismiss him. They feel that they are safer in their tenure of office upon being appointed on the permanent list, that a mere whim on the part of the minister, or an unworthy feeling, if the minister were capable of entertaining an unworthy feeling, could be exercised in an arbitrary way and they could be dismissed without any real cause. For that reason they want to get on. and they apply, and when they do, I say I will be happy to put you on and it will give me pleasure to do so, if you pass the examination. I say that to men who were years in the service before I was minister, men not in sympathy with me politically ; I treat them all alike. But there are some men who hesitate to try. and they tell me it is so long since they were at school that they could not pass the examination. but they would like to be on the permanent list. The only way we can do that is by appointing them preventive officers, and after they are appointed as such they are assigned to the duties thev have been doing for years and have been doing it well. This circumscribes the power of the minister instead of enlarging it.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) The fact seems to have been overlooked that no person over thirty-five years of age can present himself to pass the civil service examination.
Mr.i MONK. But they can be appointed preventive officers.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) And they are better qualified preventive officers than a great many who have passed the civil service examination.

The minister says that he approves of putting old and tried officers on the permanent list, but in the next breath he told us that if he did that there might as well be no examination at all. He has put a large number on the permanent list, but he has not put others who are perhaps more entitled to it.

I said that if I entertained the views of gentlemen on the other side. I would not be in favour of putting these men on the permanent list who have been ten or twelve years in office, but I do not share the opinion of lion, gentlemen opposite that it is a disqualification for a man because he does not pass the civil service examination.

The point I am making is that this Bill will enable the minister to appoint a person to a higher grade than that of a preventive officer. It

is not the desire of any one on this side of the House to interfere with the appointment of temporary officers, but it is my opinion at least that those positions which now require the examination should be protected. If the minister passes this law he will have to take the nominations made by the political committees which is now done in many cases. Probably, as the minister says none of us could pass the examination off-hand, but I am satisfied that the minister or any of us could do so if we gave it a few months study. Suppose the minister should appoint an acting officer, then although that officer might not be as good an officer as one who could pass the civil service examination, yet if there was a change of government, I for one, would certainly be opposed to removing him from an office which he had occupied for years.
Does not this amendment leave the door wide open to the minister to appoint a person to any position in the service without an examination ?
Under the present law we could appoint any person we chose as a preventive officer and continue him in the service temporarily and assign him to such duties as we may think proper.
And if this becomes law it will not be necessary to appoint a person a preventive officer, but he may be appointed to any position ?
You could appoint an acting landing waiter, but not a landing waiter.

We have the explanation of the Minister of Justice that the law now gives permission to the minister to appoint preventive officers without examination and assign them to various duties. If this clause becomes law the minister need not appoint a person as a preventive officer, but he can appoint him to discharge temporarily the duties of any position in the outside service of the Customs ?
Yes.

Then that leaves the door wide open and the minister should have the courage of his convictions and abolish the civil service examination altogether. I never myself could see why gentlemen should have to pass a qualifying examination to discharge the duties of landing waiters but, be that as it may, if the minister is logical the proper thing for him to do is to abolish the examination altogether.

There are landing waiters, tide waiters, clerks, &c. We appoint a man acting landing waiter or acting tide waiter, or acting appraiser, and give him that title ; but if he wants to become a permanent officer, and have the title of the office, he must pass the examina-12T
tion. If he cannot pass the examination, we may appoint him a preventive officer permanently, and give him the position of acting land waiter, or whatever it may be.

I have no intention of doing what I think would be an injustice, that is, touching those who, by virtue of this abuse have been in the civil service for a number of years. There is no doubt that this amendment does, not touch them ; but in case it should be so interpreted by the Minister of Customs, I will not insist upon it. But let me point this out to the hon. Minister of Justice, that I think he is mistaken in regal'd to the abuse which he contends that this section cures. Will he look at this section and tell me if, after it is passed, it will not be still possible for the Minister of Customs to name a preventive officer, and then assign to him the duties of a clerk, for instance, in a division where such a clerk would be only regularly paid $400, while the preventive officer would be drawing a much larger salary. The Minister of Justice, I am sure, has no doubt about that, because there is no doubt. It will be open to the Minister of Customs to begin by naming a man a preventive officer, and then assign to him any duties or any position he chooses, except that of deputy minister, because, as the Minister of Justice pointed out, the law does not define the duties of preventive officers. The only thing that would happen is that the Minister of Customs, without reference to the character or qualifications of the preventive officer, would name him an acting officer in one of the classes refered to. I think there is no doubt about that.
That is right.

But he would continue to name him preventive officer, and give him any salary he chose, and assign to him any functions he deemed suitable. I do not wish to continue the discussion on this point. We are breaking into the Civil Service Act by this provision. The abuse has existed in the past, and we are legalizing it. It is sufficient to refer to the Civil Service Act, sections 47a, b, c, and d, to see with what care the legislature in the past, rightly or wrongly, has surrounded entrance into the civil service, providing that if a temporary officer is employed continuously, his salary must be specially voted by parliament. All this is done away with by this clause, and 1 do not think it will effect any good.
On section 5,

Questions sometimes arise as to whether goods come under a certain designation and bear a certain rate of duty, and they are determined by the board of customs. They meet and give a decision, which, if approved by the minister, has the force of statute law, subject to an appeal of the Governor in



Council, which, however, is very seldom taken. A decision by the hoard might be contrary to what had been the practice in some ports for some time previously, and it might be that we had been collecting in some cases a higher rate of duty than that fixed by the board of customs, or in other cases a lower rate. In the former case there would be a refund, while in the latter case the importer would be asked to_ make another entry. This is to provide'that such a decision shall prevail in future, but [DOT] it shall not apply to previous transactions.
On section 6,

The present Act requires that the invoice shall be made out in the currency of the country in which the goods are actually purchased. This permits the invoice to be made out in other currency. Then there is a provision to help us better to guard against frauds.
In what cases are goods not invoiced in the currency in which they are purchased ?

The commissioner tells me that there are many cases in which the invoices of goods from the' continent are made out in sterling instead of in the currency of the country. He tells me that at times invoices are made out in Chinese or Mexican dollars.
On section 7,

I explained when the resolutions were going through what that meant. This is to provide that when au article is composed of different materials, that that component part which is of the greatest value shall determine the rate of duty.
On section 10,
Why should damaged goods be destroyed when they cannot be sold for sufficient to pay the duty ?

If a person abandons goods and will not pay the duty, we destroy them if we cannot sell them for sufficient to pay the duty. The reason is that if we destroy them other goods will come in to replace them, on which we will get the whole duty.
You are at liberty to sell them if you get enough to pay the duty, not unless you do ?
The duty is supposed to take precedence of everything else.

It is alright perhaps that the duty should take precedence. But if you can collect one-half of the duty by selling the goods, why not sell them ? The hon. minister gays that they are destroyed in order to induce the importation of other goods to take their place. That is not a good principle. Why should goods be vol-Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
untarily destroyed when their sale would realize a portion of the duties for the mere purpose of inducing other goods to be brought into the country.

I presume that the clause is all right, but I find it difficult to understand where three-fourths of the duty could be realized, the government should not sell the goods. Suppose the goods are worth $1,000 and the duty amounts to $250, according to this clause if the goods did not bring more than $225 or $200 they would have to be destroyed. I do not see why the country should lose in this way.
That has been the law for years.
Evidently the hon. gentleman has money to burn.

In my opinion, the hon. Minister of Customs is right. It would be unfair to sell the goods for a portion of the duty. Suppose the goods are valued at $1,000 and the duty amounts to $200. If you were to sell those goods and they realized only one-half thq duty, they would go into the country in opposition to other goods which paid the full duty. We want to protect the public.

I cannot see any great difference to the public in selling the goods for $200 or $199. If you can get $200 then you can sell them, but if you can only get $199 then you must destroy them, because otherwise you will injure the public by throwing them on the market. The fact that this has been on the statutes for years, does not make any difference.
On section 14,
Section 65 of the Customs Act, as amended by section 15 of chanter 14 of the statutes of 1888. is amended by adding the following subsection thereto
3. All material imported to form medicinal or toilet preparations alone or with other articles or compounds, to be put up, labelled or sold under any proprietary or special name or trade mark, shall be valued for duty under the provisions of subsection two of this section. The Minister of Customs may, however, refer to the appraising officers for valuation such of the materials as have a fair market value in the ordinary course of trade.
Is this section general or only applicable to specific articles ?
That and the next section are embodied in the Tariff Act.
Does it refer to undervaluation generally-the original clause which it is supposed to amend ?
No, not generally.

The reason I wanted to understand about this clause more particularly was that when the matter was up

a few days ago, I referred the hon. minister to the law of the United States in relation to undervaluation. I had not, at that time, the clause of the American tariff under my hand, but I have it now, and with the permission of the committee I will read it. This is the Act of June 10, 1890, section 29 article 400 :
If any owner, importer, consigner, agont or other person shall make or attempt to make any entry of imported merchandise, by means of a fraudulent or false Invoice, affidavit letter paper, or by means of any false statement' written or verbal, or by means of any false or fraudulent practice or appliance whatsoever, or shall be guilty of any wilful act or omission by means whereof the United States shall be deprived of the lawful duties or any portion thereof accruing upon the merchandise or any portion thereof, embraced or referred to in such invoice, affidavit, letter, paper or statement, or affected by such act or omission, such merchandise or the value thereof to be recovered from the person making the entry shall be forfeited, which forfeiture shall only apply to the whole of the merchandise of the value thereof in the case or package containing the particular article or articles of merchandise to which such fraud or false paper or statement relates, and such person shall upon conviction be fined for each offence a sum not exceeding $5,000 or be imprisoned for a time not exceeding two years, or both in the discretion of the court.
That is the section to which I referred in discussing this matter, and I would press upon the minister some amendment to our Customs Act of a severer character than that which exists at the present time. And I would like to know if the department intend to recommend any amendment along the lines of what I have just read ?

The Act now In force in Canada. It hardly goes so far as that read by; the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp), but I think it goes as far as the department would be inclined to recommend. It provides that, in case of smuggling or attempt to pass any fraudulent invorce or any attempt to defraud the revenue, the goods may be seized. The person fined the value of the goods, and also subjected to a penalty not more than 8200 or less than $50, or imprisonment for not more than one year or less than one month, or both fine and imprisonment.

Does not the hon. minister think the government might approach nearer the United States law-perhaps not to the extent of a fine of $5,000, but something more than the fine already imposed, which is only $200, I believe ?
' The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS. We have had cases under this law in which the judge recommended that we should not claim the full penalty of the law, saying that he had not the power under the Act to mitigate it- you get the value of the goods and $200 for every separate entry-but the accused, he thought, should not be subject to such a penalty. I think our law Is sufficiently
strong. If we are weak, it is in there being fraudulent importations we have not been able to detect.

I wish to draw the minister's attention to the large number of scales being imported iuto this country from Dayton, Ohio. I am informed of! creditable authority that these scales have been sold to the consumer for $60 or $70 each, and yet have been imported into this country at a valuation of $G or $7 each. I would ask the hon. minister if this has been brought to his attention, and if so what action has been taken ?

The matter of scales has been before us several times, and the Commissioner of Customs tells me that he is having inquiries instituted. The hon. member for Deeds and Grenville (Mr. Lavell) mentioned it the other day, and I asked him to give any names or other information that would help us to find at what port these goods had been entered. Of course, it would be outrageous to allow scales to be brought in at $6 or $7 that were sold in the regular way at $G0 or $70.
Have the scale manufacturers of Canada brought this before the department ?

I find that there have been no letters with regard to the class of scales referred to by the hon. member (Mr. Blain). The manufacturers have two or three times In the last year reported to us that scales coming from the large manufacturers-large scales-were not properly valued, and we had a special valuations made. But there has been no complaint made recently, and no complaint at all of what the hon. gentleman has referred to. It was quite new to me when it was mentioned the other night. As I say, if hon. gentlemen, or anyj one conversant with the facts will tell us at what port the entry was made or will give us any clue I shall be glad to have the matter looked up.

Before the Bill is reported, I would like to ask the minister, as the word surtax appears in this Bill, if there is any information in the possession of the government that they can give to the House and country with regard to the attitude of Germany to Canada in connection with the surtax.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W.
S. Fielding). We have nothing official. Of course we have seen the statements in the public press which the hon. gentleman has seen, but we have nothing official.
On section 17, subsection u,
For reducing the duty on any or all articles *whether natural products or products of manufactures, used as materials in Canadian manufactures ; and any such materials specified In such Order In Council shall be subject to such reduced duty of customs and no other for the time and under the conditions therein nro-vlded.

The government, as you will see, Mr. Chairman, is taking very extraordinary powers by this subsection. This matter came up when the resolutions were being discussed at a former stage. Now I want to point out to the Minister of Customs that he is seeling here a very extraordinary authority. It is no answer to say that the present law provides that you may take the duty off altogether. That is a very wide power, I admit, but it is not near so wide as the power to say what shall be the duty, dr that there shajl be no duty at all. When the hon. gentleman proposes to take power to revise the whole list of articles coming within the meaning of that section, he is asking for a most extraordinary power. Why, the hon. gentleman can revise the whole tariff so ^ far as these articles are concerned, he can fix such a scale of duties as he may think proper.
I protest against such legislation, I think it is wholly unwarranted. If a deputation comes to the hon. gentleman for some additional protection because of unfair competition by a foreign country, he may say,
I cannot take off all tlie duties, because I must have a revenue ; but I will take off some of the duties, and I will give you relief in that way. I say it is a power no government ought to have, it may be improperly exercised.
What particular class of manufactures is this proposed to affect ?
It is confined to manufactures. We have power now in the Act to deal absolutely, but it does not give the lesser power.
I want to know what class of manufactures the hon. gentleman had in his mind that this would affect.
I have not any particular class. Some Orders in Council have been passed, but I have not any particular class in my mind. But cases might arise.
Could the hon. gentleman bring us down those Orders in Council, allowing this Bill to stand in the meantime V
It will stand for the third reading.

Why insert this section if no cases have arisen ? Why this urgency V Why is the hon. gentleman reaching out his hand for more power in that direction, when he tells the committee that no cases have come under his notice that demand such authority 1

I think it fortunate that our attention has been drawn to this clause, which gives the minister such extraordinary power. He says there have been Orders in Council, we should have a memorandum of them.
There have been fifteen or seventeen.
