speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. R. Prefontaine).

speechtext:
There are several items contained in this vote, such as investigation into wrecks, removal of obstructions on navigable rivers and the winter mail service. and I may perhaps shorten the work of the committee by asking the minister to state what is the policy of the government in respect to facilitating the approach of steamers to Montreal, such as lighting the St. Lawrence between Montreal and Quebec so that it may be navigable at night. The minister has been connected with municipal affairs and with the harbour board of Montreal, and he knows the interest taken in that question. What policy does the hon. gentleman intend to follow in that respect ? Then there is the important question as to the equipment of the port of Montreal itself as to which we expect an announcement of policy. The minister will remember that last fall he took an active interest in matters concerning the port of Montreal and he wrote to the harbour commissioners inquiring what works were necessary in order that the new wharfs might be fully equipped for the handling of freight. Does the hon. gentleman intend seeing that these improvements are carried out promptly at the national expense. May we expect from the policy of the hon. gentleman that we shall make of the port of Montreal a national port. We would like to hear his opinion on that before we pass this important item. There is an item for the removal of obstructions to navigation and investigation into wrecks. The minister can do a great deal to place the port of Montreal on a better footing as regards underwriting. He is aware that the port of Montreal is now discriminated against in the matter of marine insurance. What steps does the hon. gentleman intend to take in order to place the insurance rates of the port of Montreal on a parity with the rates in American ocean ports. Then there is the question of
winter navigation between Quebec and the sea. The hon. gentleman is aware that two or three winters ago an enterprising newspaper in the city of Montreal expended quite a large sum of money in experimenting with regard to this matter. It has been urged by experts that if we employed these large ice-breaking steamers which are used by the Russian government, the season of navigation would be extended for perhaps two months longer than at present. Has the minister any policy upon that question. These are matters which it is right and proper that the minister should enlighten the committee on before we pass this item.

The item under consideration does not cover the vast field which the hon. gentleman has exploited. We are considering an item for ocean and river service now, but the hon. gentleman has spoken of the lighting of the St. Lawrence, the question of winter navigation from Quebec to the sea. and the equipment of the port of Montreal, a matter which is not dealt with in the items of the Department of Marine and Fisheries as they are before the House at the present time. However, I have no objection to answer the hon. gentleman in a general way as regards the different questions he has put. The port of Montreal is now being equipped and I hope that within this season and next season it will be capable of handling the trade of the country. As regards winter navigation, that question has been before the people for the last twenty-five or thirty years. The hon. the Senate of Canada took the matter up as far back as thirty years ago, and there are voluminous reports on the question. It was also taken up by the harbour board of Montreal to my knowledge, and a further study made of it. I think the most pressing question at the present time, not only for the port of Montreal, but for the whole country is to have the harbours of the St. Lawrence equipped in such a way that they may be able to cope with the trade that is coming to them. It is admitted on all hands that the port of Montreal (and the port of Quebec as well, for that matter) is not properly equipped. Works are going on there now as fast as possible in consideration of the means and resources of the country. I will not undertake to speak of the port of Quebec because I know a good deal less about it than I know about the port of Montreal, but as regards the 'port of Montreal, I know that since 1898 the harbour board, as-assisted by the present government, have been going on with the works there as speedily as possible. I know that the harbour commissioners of Montreal decided in 1898 to have two shifts of men, so that the work should go on day and night; and since then, with the approval of the. present government, the work has been pushed ahead in that way much more rapidly than it could have been done under the old system. It has been published that to com-

piete the equipment of the harbour of Montreal would require an expenditure of about $3,000,000, besides something more than $1,000,000 which the harbour commissioners have still available under the law passed in 1899 and 1900. They have come to the government and have asked for authority to borrow this $3,000,000 in order that the work may be proceeded with as rapidly as possible. The policy of the government will be announced in a few days, I hope, when hon. members will be in a position to discuss it. The government are alive to the situation, and I know that it is their desire to have the necessary works for the equipment of the port of Montreal completed as soon as possible, that is to say, during this season and the next season. As regards the lighting, although I should not anticipate the next item, which is lighthouse and coast service, I may say that the intention of the department
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think probably it is just as well for me to make a remark here, as nearly all these items are becoming subjects of discussion. In order that the committee may make progress, I think it would be well for hon. members to confine the discussion as nearly as possible to the item under consideration. It is quite within the right of any member to discuss almost any question under the general item of ocean and river service. Sometimes the committee agree to discuss the whole item, and then take it up item by item; but I think hon. members should confine themselves: to the item.
This is a very large vote, involving a very large sum of money-$308,600. Did I understand the Chairman to say that we must confine the discussion to each item composing the general item ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No. The rule is that the committee may decide whether they will take up each item in succession and discuss and dispose of that, or have a general discussion upon the whole vote. The hon. member can remark upon any item in this vote, and after the general discussion is over, then the committee may take up each item.
Mr. Chairman, the vote is before you in the shape of one resolution, and I have a right to put any question concerning any part of this resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is what I say. You can: put a question or discuss any of the items under this resolution.

That is what I do. I furthermore stated that I had done this in order to shorten the time-not to have to get up on all the different parts of the resolution. But there is no doubt that I can discuss any of the questions which I have discussed, under the resolution before the Chair.

I would submit that some of the questions which my Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
hon. friend has discussed are not in the resolution at all I agree with him that he can discuss any item under the resolution; but what I want to call the attention of the committee to is this, that we must take the resolution either item by item or as one vote. Our practice has been to take it up item by item. I submit that if we'do that we should confine the discussion to the one item before us. If we take the resolution up as one vote, and roam over all the items, we cannot after that take it up item by item.

I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman. Take the first item-maintenance and repairs to government steamers, $250,000. Does the hon. leader of the government contend that upon this item I cannot ask all the question which I have asked ? Surely I can ask what is going to be done about lighting the St. Lawrence, about improving the port of Montreal, about underwriting. Before we vote any money, we can bring up any question or grievance, and these are distinct grievances. If the hon. leader of the government wishes to fragmentize the discussion, it will take a longer time. Under any circumstances, it is all the one resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will read the rule, so that it may be understood. I think that a general discussion may take place on the resolution, and after the discussion each item may be taken up and dealt with. Here is the rule :
Sometimes there are a number of items in a vote or resolution, and each of these may be generally discussed as forming a part of a single question. Each item may then, if the committee think proper, be taken up as a distinct question, and so discussed and amended.

The point I make, Mr. Chairman-and I do it only in the spirit that we may not wander too far-is that my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has been discussing some questions which are not embraced in any of these items, and I hope that we shall all be confined to the subject which is immediately before us In the estimates.

In this connection, I would like to say that I have in imy room copies of the Weekly London 1 Times,' issued during the fall and winter, in which reference is made repeatedly to the unsatisfactory condition of things in the St. Lawrence; and I certainly anticipated, when my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier asked the question of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that the answer of the minister would be as to-the condition of the St. Lawrence, and what was to be done to improve the very serious condition of affairs that now exists.
I think that is quite proper.

What I want the hon. minister to do is to indicate the policy of his department and of the government on these

matters relating to navigation, and then we can take up each item, having obtained that information on the discussion of the resolution. itself.

The hon. gentleman desires that there should be a general discussion as to the policy of the government on matters not touched in this resolution. For example, he wants the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries to declare what is the policy of the government relating to the public works in the harbour at Montreal and the equipment of that port and so forth. But not one of these matters is within the scope of. this resolution. Anything touching the navigation of the St. Lawrence pertains to this item, but there is nothing in this resolution which calls for a general discussion of the policy of the government with regard to the port of Montreal.

The hon. gentleman is very severe in limiting discussion on a question raised in supply. I called the attention of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the fact that while occupying his present position, he inquired by letter from the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal what improvements they considered necessary to complete the equipment of that port. Will the hon. gentleman pretend that, when we are called on to vote the sums asked by the department, I am not entitled to ask the hon. Minister of Marine what is the policy of the government on that particular subject ?

As not one of the items in this resolution lias any relation to the improvements of the port of Montreal, I think I may contend that the hon. gentleman cannot properly bring up that subject on this motion. All I ask is that the Chairman should see that we discuss, in a broad and liberal spirit, questions within the scope of the resolutions. Questions outside that scope, important as they may be, will come up in their proper order.

I am quite ready to accept your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and I will point out to you that I asked the hon. Minister of Marine if, at the time he made that inquiry of the Montreal Harbour Commissioners, he was really carrying out the policy of the government, and if at the present moment he is prepared to inform us what is the policy of the government as regards the improvements at the port of Montreal. speechtext:
I am informed there was a report made by engineer MacMillan, saying the ship did need certain repairs, but they were not done. At any rate, whether a report was sent in or not, I know, and people competent to judge whether a Ship is fit to be on the winter service to cope with the ice, know that the ' Stanley ' was certainly in an unfit condition to cope with the ice between Prince Edward Island and the mainland last winter, and partly by reason of the neglect of the government to have her put in shape the season before, was due the disaster which resulted to shippers in Prince Edward Island last year. Now, while the ' Stanley ' was off Summe-side harbour in the ice jam, I myself, with the port warden of the town and several others, went over to examine her, and the captain himself reported that it was almost impossible to operate that steamer in the ice, because, when she went into it head on her sides were so corrugated by impact witli the ice-she is now fifteen yeas old- that she could not back up, and the steamer, on account of these defects, could work stern foremost better than she could forward in heavy ice. That is one of the causes why such a bungle was made of the winter service last year. Now, I understand the minister does not intend to send this steamer across to be fitted up this year. I would like to know where we have a ship

yard on this side where these repairs can be made. The heavy plates on the side of the ' Stanley ' will have to come oft and be straightened, and I am sure she'will not be able to take up the winter service successfully until these repairs are done. The ' Stanley ' should now be on her way across to the builders to be put in shape for next season. I asked some time ago about the loss to the shippers of perishable goods of fish and meats that were sent down to Georgetown for shipment, and on account of the defects in these boats and their not continuing the service, these fish were spoiled and had to be thrown into the field. I asked if the government had received a petition regarding a refund to the shippers for part of their losses, and the answer was that they had, and they were considering the matter. Attached to these questions there was the following memorandum and letter which I shall read to this House :
A letter has been received from the Secretary of State Department inclosing a petition from residents of Prince Edward Island who were engaged in shipping smelts and eels, asking the government to consider their claims amounting in all to $3,180.17, for fish alleged to have been spoiled during the winter season owing to the fact that the [DOT] Minto ' became disabled. It is stated that the ' Minto - was taken off the route without any notice and sent to the assistance of the ' Stanley,' and that the ' Minto ' was ice bound and helpless between the 21st of February and the 17th of March, 1903.
It is alleged that it was impossible to dispose of the goods, and consequently all the smelts and eels held at Georgetown for shipment were totally spoiled, entailing a serious loss to the shippers.
The report of agent Lord on the subject of sending the * Minto ' to the assistance of the ' Stanley ' is as follows :
I acknowledge that the result turned out very disastrous, but when this action was thought best, in the conference held in my office at which Mr. Farquharson, M.P., Captain Finlay-son, Postmaster Breeken, and others with myself were present, the steamer ' Stanley ' was and had been for over twenty days on two meals a day, and by no other means could provisions be placed on board.
And here I want to say that the ' Stanley,' before she was carried away in the drift ice from Summerside, had been ten days in the ice with ample time to provision the vessel, but the captain never sent ashore for help, for fuel or for provisions for the vessel. She was carried off down the ice in the condition that this whole House is aware of, and the steamer ' Minto ' had to be sent to her assistance, and thus the loss occurred to shippers of these perishable goods.
Her coal supply was very low, and should she be left to her fate and drift out around Cape North into the open between Cape Breton and Newfoundland the consequences might have been serious for the department, and especially this agency. Captain Finlayson's prompt assertion that it was no use for him to try Pictou Mr. LEFURGEY.
as the whole waters from Pictou light down to the east end of Pictou Island and over to the mainland on a line with Arisaig, was completely blocked with heavy ice which no steamer could break through, it was considered the only right thing to do to save the lives of the crew of the * Stanley,' and perhaps the ship.
This last statement, I would like to remark, does not correspond with the remarks of the minister when this matter was up once before, for he left this House to understand that the failure of the service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland was because the steamer ' Stanley ' was on the Summerside route. That is certainly not a fair statement when we have the captain of the ' Minto ' saying that he could not get into Pictou as the whole water from Pictou light down to the east end of Pictou Island was completely blocked with heavy ice, and that was so for a long period of time. To go on with this report of Captain Finlayson :
After consulting with Mr. Lord at the agency office and with Mr. Farquharson, M.P., we decided that the ' Minto ' should go and try to relieve the ' Stanley,' and it was not possible to get to Pictou at that time on account of the heavy drift ice jammed in between Pictou Island and Pictou, which no steamer could break through ; so we filled the ' Minto's ' bunkers and took on board about 120 tons of coal and some stores for the ' Stanley.' On the morning of the 2Sth of February we left for the 'Stanley.'
We got to the 'Stanley' about ten a.m. Before we reached the 'Stanley' Captain Brown maiked the best place to begin to break. After butting at the ice for some time, we broke in about two lengths of the 'Minto,' when the three blades of the prop slier broke otf all at once close to the hub.
Under these circnmstaEces .it is quite clear that both the agent and Captain Finlayson considered It imperative to go to the relief of the ' Stanley ' and the statement of the petitioners that the ' Minto ' could have taken perishable goods on the 21st of February and would have had no difficulty >n getting into Pictou, is not substantiated, hut on the contrary Captain Fin-layson was of the opinion that Pictou eomd not be reached. That the port of Pictou would become clear of ice in a few days afterwards, could not be foreseen. As a matter of fact the ' Minto ' had been detained in Pictou harbour from the 3rd to the 10th of February. A barrier of ice had formed across the harbour entrance and the 'Minto* could not penetrate this barrier.
As a matter of fact part of the fish was shipped to Georgetown when it was known that the 'Minto' could not reach that port
The department last January issued a public notice which was posted in manv places in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, notifying the public that perishable goods would be at the risk of the shippers. While this was intended to refer to taking goods on board the steamers yet it was sufficient notice to the public that the department would in no way consider itself liable for perisho,bin articles and that all goods intended for shipment on board the winter steamers would be entirely at the risk of the owners.
It is generally recognized principle that *when a vessel is in danger, another vessel whether a carrier of goods or not will go to

the assistance of that vessel, where lives and property are in danger, in fact if the ' Minto ' had not gone with coal and provisions to the ' Stanley ' it is probaDle that the * Stanley ' would not have been released for some time after she was released and the consequences might have been serious.
(Sgd.) F. GOURDEAU.
I would just like to read the reply to that letter of Mr. Gotirdeau from the gentleman who is the deputy port warden of Summer-side, and who is more experienced in seafaring than the hon. minister or some of his advisers. The reply is as follows
Summerside, P.E.I.. May 27, 1S03. Jas. A. Morrison, Esq.,
Summerside.
Dear Sir,-In reiply to your favour covering Mr. Gourdeau's memorandum in re the case of the fish shippers claim against the Department of Marine and Fisheries about the steamship ' Minto,' for loss of fresh fisn, 1 have to advise you, that the claim set up by the Department of Marine, is not well taken.
The ' Stanley ' was in no danger that the ' Minto ' helped her out of, as is proven by the fact that the 'Stanley' saved the ' Minto,' the latter vessel had already supplied the ''Stanley' with coal ; food could at. any time have been supplied to the ' Stanley ' and there is absolutely no question about the fact, that due diligence was not used to take the perishable goods.
The notice ' at shippers risk' cannot be pleaded, as an excuse unless due diligence is exercised by the common carrier. There is no question in my mind, but had the ' Minto ' been a private vessel instead of a government ship, a suit in court would go in favour of the shippers.
Captain Finlayson's ' prompt assertion,' that it was no use for him to try Pictou, could, in the nature of things, only apply to the then present moment, as there were ever changing conditions and there is no doubt in the mind of any person who has the capacity to judge, that the * Minto ' could have taken the perishable effects over long before they spoiled and long before the ' Stanley ' and ' Minto ' were relieved, if she had not gone to the rescue of the ' Stanley.'
In going to the rescue of the ' Stanley,' who was deserting the shippers perishable goods to have saved the other government property, therefore, on the principle of a general average claim, the thing sacrificed, has to 03 paid for by the thing protected, in short, the crew nor the ship ' Stanley ' were at aDy time in danger that other means than the ' Minto ' could not have relieved her from, it was neglect to have her short of coal or provisions at any time, for she lay off Summerside for eight days where coal contracted for by the government, was in abundance and could have been put on board : and as for provisions, and two meals per day, that was silly nonsense, I have good reason to believe that the two meals per day was a matter of convenience to the cook and to the men, who by reason of their idleness, must have suffered by eating three square meals.
The propeller of the ' Minto ' was not, I am informed, broken by the ice pan in which the ' Stanley ' was imprisoned, but by backing against a clumpet detached from it.
The evidence of the men sent to use dynamite to relieve the ' Stanley ' goes to show that they were of no value, but, that they had to
get out of the steamers way when they let her work at full speed.
I have talked with Mr. Dunn the master of the ' Jubilee,' one of the three men sent, and he declares that the ice pan could easily have been broken by the * Stanley ' if they had tried her. for in no place was the ice two feet thick.
The last paragraph of Mr. Gourdeau's letter is misleading, as in the case of the ' Minto ' and the ' Stanley,' both vessels belonging to the same owners, the recognized principle of vessels going to the assistance of others, to the loss of a third party, does not apply ; in the one case the salvors are actuated by motives the very opposite of the other, the department undertook to save their own property to the detriment of their patrons.
Captain Brown was advised by the * Port Warden ' of Summerside, in the presence of A. A. Lefurgey, Esq., M.P., that where his vessel was, off Sea Cow Head, that ice would likely break off inside of her and she would go adrift, therefore, she should have been coaled up and provisioned so as to be in readiness for any emergency, when there would have been no necessity for the ' Minto ' going to her assistance.
The 'Stanley's' drift would have been identically the same, if the * Minto ' had never went to her.
The * Stanley ' had as much coal on board when she got to Pietou as the ' Minto ' had given her.
I remain.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) JOSEPH READ, Deputy Port Warden, M.D.A., &c.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I contend that the loss to these shippers was occasioned by the 'Minto' in returning to Georgetown after the first trip she had made to the Stanley,' and taking her provisions and coal instead of taking the perishable goods, as the shippers had requested the agent of the department to do, to Pictou. The ' Minto ' made this second trip to the ' Stanley ' when there was no need of it, when neither the lives of the crew nor the safety of the vessel was in danger. As a consequence, the ' Minto ' was disabled, and it was not until the ' Stanley ' took her into Pictou that the ' Stanley ' could go back and get these goods. By that time they were absolutely spoiled. I think, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. minister, as also his colleagues, will see that the people who suffered in this regard are certainly entitled to some recompense for the loss. The amount they are asking does not cover any more than the bare cost of the goods, and is in no way compensating them for the increased value they would have had if they had been able to market them at New York or Boston, where these fish were being sent. I would further say, before sitting down, that I consider that the action of tliTs department in not sending the steamer 'Stanley ' to the old country to have the necessary repairs to her hull made [DOT]will result next year in very much the same difficulties that we have had this year. Unless the department intend putting in their estimates an amount for the building of a new winter steamer, the result to the people of Prince Edward Island will he found to be still

more disastrous. We not only want the ' Stanley ' repaired ; it is not only necessary that we shall have the ' Minto ' and ' Stanley ' to carry on the winter trade of Prince Edward Island, but it is absolutely necessary that we should have a third steamer. The business has increased to a very great extent within the last fifteen years, and we have an increasing quantity of goods for shipment each winter. When we got the 4 Stanley ' she could not cope with the trade and we had to get the ' Minto,' and now these two steamers cannot handle at. I would like to hear from the hon. minister what policy the government has in regard to fulfilling the terms of union between the island and the mainland during the coming winter.

Send her to Sorel.

Although I am new to the department yet the general rules of business should I suppose apply all over. I am informed that we have two capable officials, Mr. Stevens and Mr. Hill. we will inquire into the matter and if the facts alleged against him to-night are proved, of course there will be nothing else to be done than to dismiss him. speechtext:
I am sorry that the minister has come to such a hasty decision on the route for winter navigation.
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES I am open to conviction.

I am satisfied that when the minister is better acquainted with the circumstances which led to the disaster this last winter, he will change his opinion. If he consults his predecessor he

will be told, I think, that the Summerside-Tormentine route was most successful, as the Hon. Mr. Sutherland himself stated in the House. If the minister will take the trouble to read the speech I made some time ago he will find that it is quite certain that the miscarriage of the winter service between Summerside and Tormentine was due to the fault of the department. It is all very well to blame Mr. Lord or Mr. Finlayson or Mr. Brown, but the responsibility is on the department. Last winter was not the only winter in which the department was neglectful, but last year has been the worst under all circumstances since confederation. The breakdown of the iwiinter service was the fault of the department and- not of the route between Summerside and Tormentine. If the minister studies the facts he will not decide that Georgetown-Pictou is the only route. He will find that Captain Finlayson states in his report that for, I think, a fortnight it was impossible for any steamer to get into Pictou.
Now, the conditions which prevail to close up Pictou harbour leave Summerside and C'ape Tormentine open ; and, as I have pointed out to this House numerous times, the formation of the tides there, meeting and parting several times a day, leaves the ice always in a loose condition, and the only difficulty is in entering Summerside harbour. Suppose Summerside harbour is absolutely closed for two or three months of the year, we have asked the department to build a pier at Carleton Point; and if they do that, during the two months in the worst season, February and March, when Summerside cannot be reached, the steamer can run to Carleton Point. The distance between Summerside and Cape Tormentine is only sixteen miles, and the distance between Cape Tormentine and Carleton Point is only eight and a half miles, where the vessel can make several trips a day. So that the minister must see that the advantage is with the western route as against the Georgetown-Pietou route, where the distance is fourty miles, and where the steamer can only make one trip over returning the following day, except in extremely fine -wether. I trust that the minister will look ihto this matter this year, and that the petition for- a pier at Carleton Point will not), be left over from year to year, as ihas been done -in the past, but that the necessary amount will be brought down in the supplementary estimates for the construction of this pier. I would like to ask the minister what has been the report from the soundings taken there by the engineers just before the close of navigation.

I may say in answer to the hon. gentleman that if he has come to the conclusion that I have decided the policy of the government or the department for next winter, he is mistaken. I have expressed the opinion that, in view of the facts, it would probably be necessary to consider whether it would not be more advantageous next winter to have two steamers on the line between Georgetown and Pictou. The reason I mention this line is that it has been represented to me as the best of all the lines that have been mentioned. by one of the ex-Ministers of Marine and Fisheries, Sir Louis Davies. That is also the opinion of Captain Finlayson and Captain Brown. Under these circumstances,
I am unable to pronounce in favour of the western line. Before deciding anything, I will certainly go into the facts and circumstances, aud will moveover take the opportunity of visiting Prince Edward Island and judging for myself from the information that I gather from competent and well-informed men.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Might I ask how many trips the two steamers have made between Cape Tormentine and Summerside, that we may judge whether the trial has been fair or not ?
I am sorry I cannot give the information to the hon. gentleman ; but I will obtain it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It is very important, I think, that we should have such a communication, because the question is whether that line or the other line is the 'best. If a fair trial has not been made, perhaps it should be made, so that we may know exactly how the matter stands.

While we are speaking about the steamer ' Stanley,' I may repeat the request which I made some years ago, and which I have made nearly every session since, for a trip at the end of December between the mainland and the Magdalen islands. I think Prince Edward Island is too selfish. It ought to give a chance to the Magdalen islands, which are shut out from communication with the mainland during five or six months of the year. I have been promised years ago that the trip I request would be made. It appears that Captain Finlayson is opposed to it. I am informed by the best captains of boats, and by some reports which I have read. in the Marine and Fisheries Department, that the trip can be made. During the month of December not only is navigation between the Magdalen islands and the mainland possible, but it actually exists between Newfoundland and Cape Breton all the year round. During the month of March also the sealers from Newfoundland are seen near the Magdalen islands. I would ask the hon. minister not to forget that there is a population of 6,000 souls on the Magdalen islands, and that they deserve the consideration of the department.

The questions involved in the item before the committee are of

such great importance to the people of Prince Edward Island that I cannot allow the item to be carried without making a few remarks. The hon. member for Gaspg (Hr. Lemieux) has said that the people of Prince Edward Island are too selfish, and that they should be generous with regard io their fellow countrymen on the Magdalen islands. I want to say, Sir, that they are not selfish. We do not care if the hon. gentleman can secure a steamer for keeping up navigation with the Magdalen islands all winter. What we ask is that the terms guaranteed in the contract entered into between the province of Prince Edward Island and the Dominion of Canada shall be carried out, and that steam communication, winter and summer, shall be carried on continuously between the island and the mainland. While we do not insist on the pound of flesh, we do say that justice should be done to us, in accordance with the terms of union. With regard to the expense, we desne as much as the people of any other part of Canada to economize and save the public moneys of this country ;' but this communication is not altogether for the benefit of the people of Prince Edward Island. It has been the means of developing the trade between Prince Edward Island and all other parts of Canada.
At the time when the 'Stanley' and 'Minto' were fast in the ice, there were a hundred cars of freight at Pictou waiting to be carried across to the province of Prince Edward Island. This freight came from 1 oronto, Montreal, Quebec, Halifax and St. John, and at Georgetown there were some 80 or 90 cars of freight awaiting transhipment to die mainland. This shows the immense trade development in consequence of winter navigation having been instituted between the island and the mainland. I regret that the hon. gentleman is not disposed to send the * Stanley ' to be placed in the shipyard where she was constructed and there thoroughly repaired and refitted. It has been said that an official of the department reported in favour of sending the ' Stanley ' across the ocean for repairs. I am reminded by my hon. friend (Mr. Ross) of the facilities at Halifax for repairing ships. I may add that when crossing from Cape Tormentine to Summerside I had a conversation with engineer McMillan, who has been engineer of the ' Stanley ' the last fifteen years and who understands the condition of the steamer and the repairs required. He said that she required to go into the yard where she was constructed and where they had the proper facilities and understood what repairs were necessary She required to have her hull examined and to be thoroughly overhauled, and to have additional braces added to her frame and new plates, as the old plates were bent through contact with the ice. If these repairs were made, she would be in as good a condition as when first launched. The

government are practising false economy. Last year they spent nearly $9,000 on the repairs of the boat and she was still unfit for service. They will spend $25,000 perhaps this year on repairs again and eventually they will have to send her across to have her properly repaired in the yard where she was built. There are no facilities in Charlottetown for making the repairs. They may have them in Halifax and in Pictou and I believe that the best facilities are at Sorel. But according to Mr. McMillan, she should be sent to the yard where she was constructed and be thoroughly repaired. The hon. minister said off-hand that he believed communication will be maintained between Georgetown and Pictou next winter. That is contrary to the statement he made the other day. He said that he intended taking a trip to Prince Edward Island to view the situation for himself and then decide as to where the boats shall run. If he does that, he must arrive at the conclusion that one of the boats should be placed on the western route and the other on the eastern route. If he does that and if his captains used proper diligence and care, he will maintain a good service between the island and the mainland. Something has been said with regard to Captain Brown. It is well known that he made no efforts to extricate his ship from the position she was placed in off Sea Cow's Head. The people of Summerside walked out to the boat and asked the captain, after the boat had been only one day in the ice, what he was going to do. He said that he was not going to hire one man or pay one dollar to relieve the ship, but was going to stay there until March. This can be proved by dozens of people who boarded the vessel. Of course the ice accumulated around the boat and she was carried away with 'it and the service of the ship was lost to the people of the province. What is the result ? Claims are being made against the government for damages in connection with the frozen fish and fresh meat business. Large quantities of those products were awaiting shipment and claims have been made on tne government for about $6,000 damages on the ground, as can be proved, that the loss sustained by those shippers were largely due to the fact that proper diligence and energy were not shown in connection with thp government ships. While the amount of $6,000 may be a small sum for the government to pay as damages, to the poor men who lost their time and spent their money providing those products for market it is a considerable amount, and I trust that the government will see their way to reimbursing these men for their losses. Reference was made to Captain Reid, the port warden at Summerside. and the hon. minister rather sneered at him and would make it appear that he was a kind of a long shore sailor. Let me tell the hon. minister that Captain Joseph Reid has sailed ships on

almost every ocean, that he is a deep sea captain, that his experience and knowledge of navigation cannot he excelled by any captain either in Canada, the United State's or Great Britain, that he has the highest recommendations from the British Board of Trade, and stands first as a ship master in this country. In addition he has the confidence of at least the Liberals of the province of Prince Edward Island because they elected him to the local legislature to support the Liberal government in that province, yet the hon. minister would endeavour to east a slur on Captain Reid and the report made by him. This question is one of such importance to the people of Prince Edward Island that every effort should be made by the government to maintain winter communications. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for East Prince, the construction of a pier at Carleton Point only eight and a half miles from Cape Tormentine in New Brunswick, would obviate the necessity for another route, because it would be simply a ferry between those points, and winter and summer this communication could be maintained between Cape Tormentine and Carleton Point. There is, I understand, a measure before this parliament asking for the incorporation of a company to establish a ferry there, and pending what might be done by that company, the government should undertake to place immediately a sufficient sum in the estimates to construct a pier at Carleton Point. The engineer has been making surveys there during the first part of the winter and no doubt his report is in the department. I know that a petition from all parts of the province has been signed asking for the construction of that pier, and I trust that we will not have occasion again to discuss this matter here. I make no apology, however, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, because the question is one which not only affects the province of Prince Edward Island but the whole Dominion.

I notice that this item was 9200.000 two years ago and last year it was increased to $225,000. This year the hon. minister is asking for $250,000. I notice that the revenue two years ago was $19,000 and that last year it had fallen off to $11,000, being a decrease of $8,000. Will the hon. minister be good enough to explain this decrease when everything was so very prosperous ?

The winter before last, the revenue from the ' Minto ' and ' Stanley ' was $11,308.55. year, that is three years ago, was only $8,000, was that the service began a great deal later in the season. I want to say that up to the 12th, the time when that vessel was caught in the ice off Summerside harbour, tbe crossings at Summerside were the most successful in tbe history of the island since confederation; and had tbe captain used tbe due diligence that any private ship-owner would have used to get his vessel out of that ice, the service between Summerside and Cape Tormentine would have been kept up all winter. I cannot understand why the minister should say that it is the policy of the department to have Georgetown and' Pictou as the terminal of the winter route between the island and the mainland. I was glad to hear the minister afterwards retract those words, and state that he was going down to look into the matter himself. The people of Prince Edward Island will welcome the minister, and we trust he will look into this matter in an unbiased way, leaving out of consideration the reports of Sir Louis Davies and of Captain Finlayson, and will take the evidence we have of the tests between Summerside and Cape Tormentine, and weigh the matter carefully for himself.

I am surprised that the minister should question the advice tendered him by my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Lefurgey) in regard to possessing knowledge in reference to this question. The minister is paid to know these things. What else do we pay him for ? He is drawing now a stated salary to know something about his department in this service. We have applauded his appointment to the position he now occupies, not that we expected he possessed extraordinary knowledge in regard to marine and fisheries, but because

Sir, I fancy that the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) is entitled to have his request granted. Now, Sir, the minister has said that he does not know captain so and so, that he does not know captain this and captain that. The hon. minister has just stated that included in this item are ten or twelve boats. For these boats he must of course have supplies. If his department is not equipped in the way I am going to explain, with a store at each place, would it not be well to ask for tenders, as the Department of Public Works has done ? When the Yukon line was under way, and we wanted supplies, we called for public tenders. We got them, we opened a couple of stores, and from those stores the employees drew what they required, just as is done in the way of business everywhere else. I do not know whether the same rule is applied in the hon. gentleman's department or not; but when supplies to the amount of $40,000 and 14,000 tons of coal are to be bought, I think it would be a good rule to follow. Then each boat would draw from the stores what it required, as is done in any well organized business. I think that suggestion is worth looking into. Is the hon. gentleman in a position to tell us whether such a rule has been applied ?

I am informed that the rule has not been applied at all, for the simple reason that the supplies are bought at the different

places as they are wanted at the lowest market price, and the provisions are ordered through the agent. Most of the coal required in the maritime provinces is bought at the mines.

speechtext: I speak in a general way. The hon. gentleman, I have no doubt, would he in a position to ask his officers how much butter, how much pork, how much beans, how much flour, would be required for such and such boats. I think it would be a very good rule to follow if it has not been followed in the past. The goods for Halifax would be delivered there and the goods for Quebec would be delivered at Quebec. That was what the Department of Public Works did in the Yukon. We asked for public tenders, the goods to be delivered at Vancouver, at White Horse, and so on. I am just asking the hon. gentleman to follow a system which I followed myself. If it is not applied in his department, I think it should be applied there. These are pretty large amounts of money to spend for supplies, although I quite grant that if the coal is bought at the mines, he could not perhaps do better. But, all the same, when 14,000 or 15,000 tons are required, I think public tenders should be asked.

I do not think my hon. friend is right in assuming that there is any difference in the method of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries Department and that of the Public Works Department. When he speaks of public tenders, does he mean tenders by public advertisement ?
We did that for the Yukon.
I think that to a certain extent my hon. friend is mistaken, for in some instances, for the supplies for the Yukon tenders were invited by circulars.
No, what took place was this. We asked for public tenders first. Prices were sent in, and goods were obtained for one year. Last year the contract was renewed at the same prices.
I think ray hon. friend is mistaken if he implies that that was done by public advertisement in all cases. I am quite satisfied that his tenders for supplies were obtained by circulars.
Yes, for small amounts.

There has been no change in the method of ordering supplies in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The method is the same as Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
that which prevailed in former years. The only question is whether the supplies have been obtained at fair and reasonable prices. That is a proper question for inquiry in the Public Accounts Committee. I am quite satisfied that every article has been ordered in good faith and under the fullest supervision, and we challenge the most thorough investigation in the Public Accounts Committee as to whether the prices paid are fair and reasonable. As to issuing public advertisements for tenders for the supply of coal, what would be the use of putting advertisements in the newspapers 1 There are only half a dozen mines in Nova Scotia, and when coal is to be supplied at Pictou, you would hardly bring it from Sydney or Cumberland. You would necessarily get it from the mines in the locality where it was wanted, and I am satisfied the prices are obtained from the various mines in that locality. So in every other case the effort is made to get the goods required at fair and reasonable prices.
Do I understand the bon. minister to say that he sends out circulars for everything required at the opening of navigation ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: And that a price is then made ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: And that price is the same all the year round ?
Yes, all the year round.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: If circulars are sent out in large numbers, the system is not as bad as it might be. Will the hon. Minister of Finance permit me to say that I am not far from the mark in stating that if public tenders were asked when large amounts of provisions are wanted, twenty-five or thirty per cent would be saved. In the Yukon we had the very same experience. We started buying, just in the way pointed out now. Later on we invited tenders, and prices went down. I was criticised in the Public Accounts Committee, as it was the right of the opposition to criticise me. I am not far from the mark in stating that if public tenders were asked, say for meat, tea, coffee, and a group of merchandise, to be delivered at Halifax, Quebec or elsewhere, the department would save trouble and criticism for itself, and save money for the country.

I can neither admit nor deny my hon. friend's statement with reference to the Yukon, because I admit that he has a better knowledge of that than I have; but, as respects these supplies, if he thinks he could save

twenty-five or thirty per cent, I am bound to say I differ from him. I do not think my hon. friend will say that when he ordered goods in the Department of Public Works by circular, we thereby lost from twenty-five and thirty-five per cent. No doubt he believed that by that method he obtained fair and reasonable prices, and if that were possible in the Public Works Department it is equally possible in the Marine and Fisheries Department. I know as a matter of fact that in some of the ports where these supplies are furnished, they are obtained at very moderate terms-so much so that people hardly care to compete for the furnishing of them. Take the case of Halifax, of which 1 have personal knowledge, the agent of the Marine and Fisheries Department there is a gentleman who has been in the service many years, and who has certified that every item in the account is charged at a fair and reasonable price. I am sure that he would not certify to items that were charged at from twenty-five to thirty-five per cent over what is fair and reasonable.
Would it not be worth trying ?
Why more to-day than when my hon. friend was minister ?
Hear, hear.

My hon. friends opposite say hear, hear, but two blacks do not make a white, or two whites a black. It is a question of business, and business men will, I believe, share in the views I have just expressed. So far as the Yukon telegraph is concerned, there was a large amount involved, and if I remember aright, some of my colleagues were of the opinion that public tenders should be asked, and I asked for public tenders. I remember very well that in the Department of Public Works at Ottawa, when small amounts were in question, we asked for prices by circular, but these were very small amounts indeed. However, I have called the attention of the minister to this point, and do not want to insist on it. Now that I am on my feet, might I ask the hon. gentleman whether he has made any inquiry as to the reasons why the ' Stanley ' could not maintain the winter service between Sum-merside and the mainland-whether there is any official report on that question.
The papers were all laid on the Table two months ago.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman give, in a few words, the reasons why the efforts were unsuccessful ?
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND
FISHERIES. It is well known that the
failure was due to the weather. The question came before the House and all the facts were explained. The ' Stanley ' was caught in such heavy ice-as thick as four and a half feet-that it was impossible for her to move either one way or the other. That is why the ' Minto ' was called to her assistance, but unfortunately, she broke three blades of her propeller and was disabled. It was only after two or three weeks that the ' Stanley ' succeeded in extricating herself from the ice and she towed the ' Minto ' to the port of Pictou. It was an accident quite uncontrollable.

Statements have been made in the House that no efforts were made to work the boats. I was very much surprised, because to my knowledge the steamers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries are very well manned as a rule, and good discipline is maintained on board. I have visited them often and am glad to say that no steamers could be better kept. What I wanted to know was whether any inquiry has been held regarding the statements that the captain made no efforts.
The MINISTER OF MARiNE AND FISHERIES. He made every effort, and it is quite clear to the department that the accident was unavoidable.

I would like to suggest, in answer to what has been said by the hon. Minister of Finance, that it does not seem much of an argument against the advertising of the supplies that the ex-Minister of Public Works did not always do it. There does not seem to be much cogency in that argument. There would, however, seem to be more force in the statement of the ex-Minister of Public Works that having tried both systems, he thinks there will be very considerable saving if the system of advertising in the newspapers be adopted. If the supplies can be obtained in that way, what is the objection ? I have heard something in Nova Scotia about the way these circulars are sent out, and the information that has come to me is that they are given a very restricted circulation, much more limited than was the case under the late administration ; and as far as my hon. friend's observation with regard to the Committee of Public Accounts is concerned, he knows that if the committee sat every day, instead of once or twice a month, as it has been doing, it would not be able to make any such investigation of these items as would justify the removal of any public safeguard. Under the circumstances, I cannot see any force in the observations of m.v hon. friend or any possible objection to putting advertisements in the newspapers with regard to supplies required by the departments.

I believe that we have experienced no difficulty in the past in having investigations before the Committee of Public Accounts. During last

session a very considerable portion of the time of that committee was taken np in answering the criticisms of hon. gentlemen opposite on expenditures in the Department of Public Works, which were held to be rash and extravagant, just as the expenditures now being criticised are considered to-day. But upon full investigation, these charges were found absolutely unjustified, and I believe that an investigation to-day with respect to the Department of Marine would have precisely the same result. It is easy, in this House, to make general statements that purchases are extravagant, but these have not borne investigation successfully in the past and will not in the future, I am satisfied. As regards the method followed in former years, the government in former years purchased these supplies from their friends, and I presume the present government does so. Why should we not be frank on that subject ? There is no change in the system and the only question is whether the prices are fair and reasonable. If purchasing from friends of the government leads to excessive prices, that is an abuse which no practice in the past can justify, but unless the hon. gentleman can show that the prices are excessive and that these certificates given by men like Mr. Lord, of Charlottetown ; Mr. Parsons, of Halifax ; Mr. Harding, of St. John, and others, are false, it is not fair to assume that there is any extravagance in the prices.
I hope my hon. friend will not put in my mouth words that I had no intention of using. I never charged the Department of Marine with extravagance.
Others have.

I was speaking for myself. I have that right-the only one that may be left me. I did not want to make any change of the kind, but was speaking in a general way, and I spoke, I think, the language of a sound business man. The hon. gentleman says truly that the government have a right to favour their friends. But there are certain limits to that right. Governments should not go beyond these limits. For instance, it would be very pleasant to be able to give contracts for wharfs and lighthouses without tenders, but they do not do it. We ask for public tenders.
Why ?

Because the law is there. The spirit of the law is that when a large expenditure is to be incurred, as a rule tenders are publicly called for. I was simply speaking in that direction. Here is an expenditure of $40,000 or $50,000, and I suggested that perhaps the country would save money by publicly asking for tenders. But if the hon. minister is satisfied that Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
there is no money to be saved he is responsible for his statement. I am responsible for mine.

There is no doubt but that the Minister of Finance is absolutely mistaken, and so is the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. When the Minister of Finance says that an investigation is necessary to show that we could save 25 or 30 per cent on these purchases he is mistaken. That investigation has been made, and we find the results in the Auditor General's Report for last year. If hon. members will take the trouble to consult that report as to the purchases of supplies for government steamers, they will be persuaded, not that we could have saved 30 per cent only, but that we could have saved 40 or 50 per cent at least upon provisions had we called for tenders publicly. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries says that circulars were issued, and that a comparison shows that fair market prices are secured. I shall not take the trouble to read the Auditor General's Report, but if hon. members will take the trouble to read it, they will find that the saving would be as great as I have said.

They are not all bought in the same place.
Mi'. MONK. Because the hon. minister will not carry out the rule the adoption of which we are advocating. Take the case of groceries, for instance. Surely it would be possible for the minister to call for tenders for groceries to be furnished during the summer season to the government steamers. Here in the Auditor General's Report, beginning at page P-9, the hon. minister will find instances where groceries have been bought by the thousand pounds at as high prices as we pay at retail in Montreal. In the city of Montreal we have, as other cities have, large wholesale houses that would be glad to tender for these supplies, and-1 am speaking of groceries only-would be able to supply the country at a saving of 40 per cent on the prices that have been paid. How, then, can the Minister of Finance say we must make an investigation before the Public Accounts Committee to establish what is here proven ? The same thing applies to the furnishing of green groceries, and the same thing to hardware. I am not as conversant with hardware, but I venture to say that if tenders were publicly called for we would gain over 30 per cent. Why not let it be done 5 It is no answer for the minister to say it has not been done in the past. The public expenditure is increasing and we are here to call attention to the existence of wise rules. There can be no doubt in the mind of any reasonable man that in articles that are required in large quantities-cwlien it is a question of a few dollars' worth
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: We could not do it.

We could not do it-but, in au expenditure of $40,000, we could save $15,000. I think that the hon. minister, now that he is just taking hold of his department, should apply this rule in purchasing supplies for the steamers. This is reasonable. Then why not do it 7

There is this difference between the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and myself : When he says that 30 or 40 per cent could be saved on these purchases, he assumes that his mere saying it proves it ; on the other hand, I confess I cannot accept that reasoning at all.
I can give instances.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) cannot give instances, because he has no knowledge of the circumstances under which these purchases take place. What I do know is that in all these cases-I am speaking generally-reputable officers, many of them appointed under former governments, certify, with respect to these items, that the prices are fair and reasonable. This is the evidence of a man on the spot, a man whose duty it is to know the facts. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier says that we must dismiss that and take his own statement to the contrary. I do not think that is fair.

I can cite one instance that came under my notice since I became a minister. Circulars were sent out in the city of Quebec for the purchase of provisions for two or three steamers there. We received about twenty tenders, and the articles which were lowest were chosen from the different tenders. Our agent there reported as to every article that he recommended to be bought from the different tenderers that the prices were reasonable according to the current market prices. Our officer has been there for thirty years, and is in a position to know the facts. Of course, there are articles for which tenders cannot be had, for instance, the articles the supplies of which are bought daily. In that case, our agent is directly responsible, because he must certify that the prices paid are not higher than the market prices. Two years ago, a great fuss was made about some bread furnished in Quebec for the steamers, which appeared in the Auditor General's Report as being double the price of bread bought in Halifax. After investigation, it was discovered that the loaves of bread in Halifax were a certain number of pounds, while the loaves in Quebec were double that weight, explaining at once the difference in price. Another point was made that brick had been bought at $40 a thousand when ordinary brick was selling at $7 or $8 a thousand. It was discovered that a few fire brick had been imported to repair a furnace, and they had been paid
for at the regular price in the market. As regards coal, as I have explained, it is bought in different places. In the maritime provinces, it is usually bought at the mines, and the prices are the lowest at which coal can be bought. In Quebec and other places where we are not near the mines, circulars are sent out calling for tenders. The prices are compared by the agent with market prices, and he takes the responsibility of certifying that they are fair and reasonable.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Why does the hon. minister say that coal is bought at the mine ? Is it not delivered at the steamer's side ?
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND , FISHERIES. Delivered at the steamer. But bought from the producer. Take Pic-tou, for instance. The coal bought at Pictou was all got by tender at the mines for $3.75 fob on the wharf. At Sydney we paid $3.
How many steamers are coaled at Pictou ?
It depends entirely on when they pass there. Sometimes they would coal two or three times in the summer. One may coal three or four times and another only once.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is the contract invited for the whole season ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: When the minister says bought at the mine, does he mean purchased from the mining company, or [DOT] purchased at the mine through some agent ? In other words, is there any commission on this $3.75 for coal at Pictou ?

It was purchased from the Intercolonial mine by tender. At Halifax it was purchased for $4.75, there is no mention from whom it was bought. At Sydney it was bought from the Dominion Coal Company at $3.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not know whether the minister is aware of it, but I have understood that sometimes in these public contracts the full weight of coal does not always materialize. What steps has the minister taken to see that the coal is delivered in proper weight ?
I have not heard there is any deficiency in the weight.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
The Minister of Finance has made an argument that seems to me so puerile that it is not worth while answering. He says that when he has a certificate from an officer of the government that the goods have been delivered and that the prices charged are reasonable, that ought to be

sufficient, tender or no tender. Let me tell the Minister of Finance that if he will take the /last report of the Auditor General, at page F-9, he will find a purchase amounting to $580.57, made at Quebec for groceries, at prices for every article that far exceed the prices we pay in Montreal in retail stores, even the largest stores. Is the minister going to pretend that if he calls for tenders for large supplies of those articles giving every man in the Dominion who is in business a chance to tender, he would not get them cheaper ? I venture to say that that item of $588 would be reduced to less than $350. I can find numberless instances. For instance, here is coffee, 40 cents at one place, 35 at another, more or less at another; when we can get it for 30 cents, of the very best quality, in Montreal from wholesale grocers if they were allowed to tender. There is no question about the principle. The question is that the minister is asking us for $250,000, and he will not pledge himself that the citizens of this Dominion will have a chance to tender as the law requires.

I say there is no such law, that is my first point. In the second place, the hon. gentlemau quoting coffee at 40 cents a pound, does not prove anything at all. There is coffee and coffee, everything depends on the quality and on circumstances. No doubt many a man in this House pays more than 40 cents a pound for coffee, and does not consider that he is being robbed. Everything depends on the circumstances under which the goods are supplied, the quality of the goods, the condition of the market, and many other things of which my hon. friend cannot possibly have any knowledge. But if on any of these goods we have information that the prices are excessive, I am sure that on inquiry we will be glad to have his assistance in showing it. But we should not assume that the prices are excessive upon any such information as he has yet given us.
Can the Minister of Marine and Fisheries tell us whether he has asked tenders from wholesale men ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman asked for tenders by circulars from wholesale grocers such as Martin & Co., or Chaput & Co., there would not be great objection. But let me assure him that if he looks carefully into the report of the Auditor General he will find that on many occasions, not only in his department, but in others, things are bought at retail prices. That should not be done. Last year I was placed in that same position. I will mention one fact which the Minister of Finance will remember. We had asked for tenders by circular in British Columbia for the Yukon telegraph. Prices came down here that we regarded too Mr. MONK.
high. I applied to some wholesale grocers in Montreal, Martin & Co. and Chaput & Co., three or four wholesale grocers, and I found it advantageous to buy in Montreal and to ship the goods to Vancouver. The Department of Public Works has a record of that. Now the Minister of Finance should not lose sight of these facts. These are hard facts that no argument can gainsay; and my hon. friend is wrong when he lays down as a principle that when the certificate of a local man, of the engineer or the foreman, is on the paper, it should be taken for granted that the prices are right. I am speaking after an experience of nearly six years and a half as Minister of Public Works, and I state boldly that if the chief officials of the department here did not control the certificates of their local men, there would be abuses that the Minister of Finance has no idea of. He has no conception of the abuses that would prevail if the chief officers of the department did not control the certificates of the local men. I have been caught myself unwillingly, my officers have been caught unwillingly on several occasions. This is not a rule that should be followed, and I do not think the Minister of Finance means that it should be absolutely followed. If the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will follow my suggestion he will save money for the public treasury. Let him ask for prices from wholesale firms in several places. Every business man would ask for tenders from wholesale houses in several towns and cities, knowing that he would then get fair prices. My hon. friend said a moment ago that the price of coffee in Montreal is 30 cents. I am buying my coffee at this moment for 30 cents a pound, the best coffee in Montreal.
I do not like that coffee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I can assure him that I know what good coffee is. For 30 cents a pound you can get the best coffee in the Montreal market.

With regard to these certificates that prices are fair and reasonable, the hon. gentleman seems to assume that his officers in the Public Works Department kept their eyes on these certificates, and that there were no officers in the Marine and Fisheries Department who do likewise.
No, I did not mean that at all.

The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has officers to supervise these accounts, and if there seems to be anything excessive, either in the Public Works Department or in the Marine and Fisheries Department, undoubtedly it would be the duty of the higher officers to call attention to it. All I claim is that when you have that certificate from a reputable officer,
I

it is prima facie evidence that the prices are fair and reasonable until somebody shows to the contrary.

I did not accuse the officers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries more than any one else,' nothing of the kfnd. I am only laying down a principle that I believe is sound. I believe that the officers of the Marine and Fisheries Department are just as good as any other officers ; to my knowledge they are" honest men, and I have nothing to say against them, far from it.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) X know something about wholesale groceries in the city of Halifax, and I would say that in no instance can it be found that there is 5 per cent or 10 per cent overcharge. If the hon. gentleman will look at the prices in the city of Halifax he will find that the government has been supplied at as reasonable prices as would be charged any other buyer, because these purchases are made by men of the highest reputation. X know, that, in the case of hardware, some Halifax merchants stated to me that they would sooner not have supplied these goods that they would have done better by filling their own orders all over the country, because the prices have been reduced so low that there was no inducement for them to supply these goods to the government vessels. If you go minutely through the list of supplies that have been furnished at the port of Halifax you will find that in no instance has there been an overcharge. I know that coal is supplied by the mines of Cape Breton and shipped on board vessels to be carried here and there at the very lowest price. This year a case came under my own personal knowledge in which coal was supplied as low as three years ago.

My hon. friend from Victoria, N.S. (Hon. sir. Ross) says that hardware was bought at a very low rate in Halifax. I have under my hand the accounts for a quantity of goods known as software that was purchased for the ' Minto ' in the port of Halifax, and I would like to read it for the benefit of the committee :
James Scott & Co., Halifax : Soda water, ginger beer, apollinaris and lemonade, fourteen dozen, $14.10.
X would like to know if this is a fair price for soft goods in Halifax. As the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries is in the habit of issuing a circular inviting tenders he no doubt issues a schedule of quality stating the kind of goods required. I notice in the Auditor General's Report at page P-26 the following charge :
Sanderson & Co., Charlottetown, Turkish cigarettes, two tins, $4.75 per tin.
I would like to ask the hon. minister whether he received a tender for Turkish cigarettes, and if he would consider that was a fair price or not and I would like to
ask him in what way Turkish cigarettes are used in the navigation of steamships ? I think he at least must have added $2 a tin to the ordinary price of Turkish cigarettes on that occasion. I would like to know how many tenders he received for the supply of these cigarettes and if the offer of Sanderson & Co., of Charlottetown, was the only one received, and if this government vessel could not have proceeded on its voyage just as well without these cigarettes.

The hon. Minister of Finance said that we would find a variation in prices in the different localities in which supplies were purchased. Of course, we may be critical in regard to these matters, but it is the duty of an opposition to ascertain the facts in connection with public expenditure. I would not say that for every expenditure of $500 the rule of advertising for tenders must be observed, but where it means an expenditure of a considerable amount of money the government must allow that it is open to criticism and at least to suspicion if tenders are not invited. It is not necessary for us to go through all these items that are contained in the Auditor General's Report. It is impossible for the members of this committee as a whole to attend the Public Accounts Committee. It is impossible for us to investigate. If we did attend the Public Accounts Committee, the expenditure of this government in all its departments, as it is represented in the report of the Auditor General, and if we were to follow the rule laid down by the hon. Minister of Finance, we would be confronted at once by the statement that we had got all these particulars in the Public Accounts Committee. I am sure the lion. Minister of Finance will not lay it down as a principle that we should not criticise any detail of the expenditure in any department unless we had investigated it in the Public Accounts Committee, because that would be a principle impossible to carry out. The Public Accounts Committee would have to .sit year after year and this House never would rise if we were to follow out that principle. Taking up the question of a single item, I will give the committee a comparison of the prices charged for the article of potatoes. I find that at Rimouski there was a charge of 40 cents a bushel, at St. Andrews, a charge of $2 a Bushel, at Shelbourne, 50 cents a bushel, at Souris, 33 cents a bushel, at another place 00 cents a bushel, at another place $2 a bushel.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Would that not be $2 a barrel ?

Two dollars is a little high, Mr. Ross, even under your administration. At another place 60 cents a bushel, at another place 78 cents a bushel, and so on all through you find this variation in connection with that article. Even if I had the long long years of training of my hon. and venerable friend from Victoria, N.S., I do not think

that I could accept a variation between 33 cents and $2 a bushel without making an inquiry of the hon. minister. I would not be expected to go to the Public Accounts Committee to warrant me in rising in my seat and criticising such items as these. Now, Sir, all this criticism and all this suspicion can be avoided if the better system were followed of calling for public tenders. 1 am sure that we would accept it from the hon. minister as being more or less satisfactory if he would say to-night that in future, he will adopt the system of asking for public tenders in connection with the general supplies required by this department. It is quite easy after the years of experience we have had in operating these steamers and it would be very businesslike also for the department to make an estimate based upon the expenditure of years gone by of what the requirements would be in the year to come in the various articles such as groceries, coal, &c. That is only business. It is done by every business firm in Canada or in the world, so far as that goes, and it is very easy for the hon. minister to make a reasonable estimate of the supplies that would be required and ask for a public tender for the quantity needed during the year. Let him advertise for these tenders and when he receives these tenders let him act upon them without any undue influence, which I am sure would not be exercised by the hon. minister and if he did this the duty of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House would be simple. It would be much easier and more satisfactory for all of us. When we look through these items and find the wonderful variation in price which no distance warrants we are certainly justified in protesting against such a system as this. There is no distance in all of Canada that warrants a difference between 33 cents and $2 a bushel.
Is it $2 a barrel or .$2 a bushel ?
It is $2 a bushel.
It is six barrels at $2 a barrel.

They may have been seed potatoes, but there is entered here one bushel at $2. If the hon. gentleman thinks he scored a bull's-eye, let him take his prize. The gentlemen on this side of the House would be absolutely derelict of their duty if they did not absolutely protest against the method of purchasing these articles and the prices paid for them. The minister is starting in a larger sphere as a responsible minister of the Crown, and it would be to his credit if he would get up now and state that in future these supplies will be obtained by public tenders. Is he going on with the old system of buying these supplies in future as in the past, or will he invite tenders ?
Carried.
No, it is not carried. I have asked a fair question, and I want an answer.
It is not my intention to change the system.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We paid F. X. Drolet, of Quebec, $6,663.51, and I want to know whether we bought from him by tender or if the prices he charged were what he thought fit to charge ? We have an item here for rope specially made for steering gear, 130 feet at 50 cents per foot. That is an outrageous price for a foot of rope.

I am informed that this party is a machinist, and that it is an account for the work and material he has furnished for the steamer in the regular way.
Mi-. TAYLOR. This work was not done by tender ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: There could be no tender for such repairs as that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Who are the wholesale grocers in Quebec from whom he asked tenders ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. They are mostly all asked, but I know the firm of Turner.

A very good firm it is. You say that tenders were asked from Whitehead & Turner ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Yes, and they got part of the contract.

Who were the other firms ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. There were twenty. As far as I can remember, there were amongst others Coleman, and Dion, and Thibaudeau.
Dion is not a wholesale grocer, and Coleman is not a wholesale grocer, either.
Yes, he is.
Do these boats carry passengers ?
Those which do the winter service to Prince Edward Island carry passengers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
