speechtext: There are many charges of luxuries of a very expensive character, and if they did not carry passengers and supply meals, these items would be very extraordinary.
The Prince Edward Island steamers supply meals.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The expenditure on these boats is $452,526; now what is the revenue from these boats ?
The revenue, as I have already given, from the ' Minto ' and ' Stanley ' was for 1901-2 $11,308, and this year from the ' Minto ' $11,111.57. and from the ' Stanley ' $4,178.40, making $15,289.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: So that while the total expenditure of the department on these boats is $450,000, we have a revenue from them of about $15,000. The hon. Minister of Finance approves of the principle of purchasing supplies laid down for years by both parties ; but I beg to differ from him with regard to that principle. I contend that a government party have a perfect right, when they ask for tenders, all things being equal, to give the contract to their friends ; but it is no answer to say that they have purchased supplies from their friends and paid a reasonable price for them. The only true principle is, first, to call for tenders, and then, all things being equal, to give the contract to your political friends. When the government go outside of that principle, they are not doing what I believe to be in the best interests of the people of this country. When you look over these items, notwithstanding the statement by the hon. member for Victoria that men are to be found who are so patriotic in spirit towards the Depai-tment of Marine and Fisheries. that they furnish things for less than cost

I made no such statement. I repeat the statement I made. I confined myself to the port of Halifax, because I do business there, and know something of the character of the gentlemen who supply these articles.
If the hon. gentleman will turn to page P-26 of the Auditor General's Report, he will find a large number of items there for which excessive prices were paid.
By whom supplied ?

By Sanderson & Company, of Charlottetown ; and by James Scott & Company, of Halifax.
Mr. ROCHE (Halifaxl. Give the prices.

I do not wish to take up the time of the House unnecessarily ; but I will give a few : Bananas, 2 bushels, $5.75 ; fancy biscuits, 15 pounds at 20 cents ; pilot biscuits, 384 pounds at 7 cents ; breakfast and dinner biscuits, 13J pounds at 50 cents ; sugar and opera wafers, 1 dozen, $5.50 ; Turkish cigarettes, 2 tins, $4.75 ; crystallized fruits, 20 pounds at 60 cents ; figs in cordial, Indian relish, stuffed olives, truffles. I could quote many other things.
Go on.
If the hon. gentlemen want me to take up a few hours here I will do so.
Yes, go on.
Do the hon. gentlemen wish to listen to me for a few hours ?

Yes, certainly.
Mi-. INGRAM. I shall be very glad to entertain them if they wish. I did not rise for that purpose this evening. I would rather assist the Minister of Finance in getting through the estimates ; but on some other occasion I will be glad to entertain them.

My hon. friend has mentioned the name of a reputable Halifax firm, and has conveyed the impression that that firm charged extravagant prices. I know the members of that firm, and I am satisfied that they would not charge a price that was not fair and reasonable, and if the circumstances are investigated, I am sure this will be established. It is not fair for hon. gentlemen to convey the impression that a reputable firm had charged extravagant prices unless they are prepared to establish it.

Does the hon. Minister of Finance think the people of Canada should pay for these luxuries to be furnished to the men employed to run these boats ? Why are we called on to furnish them with cigarettes ? I do not think this is a laughable matter at all. The question is why the ratepayers of Canada should pay for these luxuries; and when the price paid for coffee is pointed out, what answer do we get from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries ? A very jocular and laughing answer, that he did not drink thirty cents coffee. Weil, I am willing that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or any one else should drink as expensive coffee as he pleases if he pays for it himself ; but I do not believe the ratepayers of Canada are required to buy the best things in the market
Carried.

No, it is not carried ; and the gentlemen might as well keep their mouths shut. I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite that I represent a constituency, and I am not going to be bull-dozed by any of their horse laughs at anything I am saying. What I was saying is, why should we be called upon as ratepayers of the Dominion of Canada to furnish luxuries for the men working the boats on the St. Lawrence or the Atlantic ? I do not think we are called on to furnish cigarettes, these delicate waters, and all this other stuff to men in every-day life. I do not blame the hon. Minister of Finance so much, because he was not in this House, but he is advocating quite a different principle to-night from that which his party advocated when in opposition. If the prin-

ciple was not a good one when we were in power, can he say, in any fairness, that it is a good one now ? The hon. gentleman's friends strongly denounced this practice in the past, but those gentlemen are doing the very same thing now which they condemned then. They are doubly guilty- more than that, they are hypocrites. There is the Postmaster General, he remembers when he was in opposition.
Tell us what I said.

I would not use the language you did in parliament. We never descended on this side to criticising items such as the washing of napkins and that sort of thing at Government House. We never criticised on this side of the House the Prime Minister's livery bill. Our criticisms are on a higher plane. I would not descend to criticise the washing of napkins at Government House when I was invited to dine there and helped to soil them. We are called on to furnish luxuries for gentlemen managing these boats. We are spending thousands and thousands of dollars in buying these luxuries, which the ordinary ratepayer of Canada is not able to purchase for his own table. As a representative of a rural constituency, I protest against this expenditure on luxuries, which the great bulk of my electors are not in a position to purchase for their own families. We had better call a halt on this line. Does it follow that because we made mistakes in the past and did not call for tenders, this business administration, which has been heralded all over the country as a business administration, should do the same thing.

We have had the assurance several times during the debate that these prices must be all right because the officials of the government have certified to that effect, and we have been challenged over and over again to point out particular items of over charge. Let me call attention to a few items which will be found on page 22-P of the Auditor General's Report. On the very first line, I find, among supplies furnished to the steamer ' Minto,' 985 pounds of beef at 10 cents; six pairs of chickens at one dollar; 799 pounds of mutton at 12 cents. Hon. gentlemen from Summerside can say whether these are fair prices or not. Beef 10 cents per pound; eggs, 25 cents per dozen; Royal Baking powder at 55 cents, an article which is put up at 25 to 30 cents; sardines, two dozen at SI'90 per dozen; salmon, two cases at $7.75; vinegar, 75 cents per gallon. It is well known that the very best domestic vinegar can be bought at 4o cents per gallon, and give a handsome profit to the retailer. All through you have the evidence that these gentleman who certified to these prices are just figure heads and would certify to anv-thing.

That is a very grave accusation. Very much depends on the circumstances under which these goods are ordered. It is not possible from the mere reading of the figures from the Auditor General's Report, to form any conclusion, without a knowledge of the circumstances. With regard to the luxuries, I know the circumstances under which the cigarettes were purchased and they cost $2 or $3, but the other articles are only such as would appear on the table of the commonest railway restaurant in the Dominion. You will find India relishes and things of that kind on the table of any restaurant and they are not luxuries in a ship which carries passengers.	[DOT]
They do not carry passengers.
Yes, they do. They are not luxuries in the sense in which the hon. gentleman says they are.
I was quoting the prices of necessaries.
My hon. friend who spoke before the bon. gentleman spoke of luxuries.
Here is a charge for beef, 985 pounds at 10 cents. I am informed that it is an article which can be bought at 0 or 7 cents. Mutton at 12 cents is surely an exorbitant price.

Will any one pretend that we could not buy sugar in large quantities at less than five cents per pound. Here is one firm which charges five cents per pound. Everybody knows that that is an excessive price. Tea, coffee and sugar are staple supplies which you could buy in large quantities, and distribute to these vessels as required. I could understand your paying excessive prices at certain points for perishable articles such as bananas, but the staple articles you should purchase in large quantities and under contract. I do not care what the past system has been, the present system should be changed. The system of the past was a wrong system and there is no reason why it should be continued. If the government change the system there will be no reason for such complaints as have been made to-night. But, in relation to such a system as we now have, the criticism is perfectly proper. It is clearly in the interest of the country that the system should be changed.

There may be much in what the Minister of Finance said with regard to the condition under which the articles are purchased. But, when I find that in the city of Quebec a purchase of 984 pounds of sugar was made at five cents per pound, another purchase of 349 at five and one half cents and, from another grocer, 296 pounds at five cents per

pound, it seems quite evident that there is something wrong. The conditions at Quebec are much more favourable for the purchase of sugar than the conditions in western Ontario. Now, I speak of something of which I have practical knowledge when I say that in western Ontario thirty-five miles west of Toronto, after paying water freight and inland freight by rail, sugar one year ago-the time when these accounts were made up-was sold to the farmers of that section at a profit at four cents per pound. This was standard granulated No. 1, and I have no doubt that the sugar here referred to was not one whit better, for it is a standard article. It is evident, that, as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier said, in that item alone the price is from twenty-five to thirty per cent above actual value. With many other articles there may be differences. The hon. member for Grey (Mr. Richardson) referred to baking powder. That is sold at varying prices. He also referred to vinegar, the price of which is well known. I think the hon. gentleman is within the mark in saying that for such an article as would be required on board a steamer 30 cents or 40 cents would be a fair price, and it is astonishing to find an entry here of ten gallons of vinegar at 75 cents or five gallons at 60 cents. Now, take another article the value of which we all know-fresh water. In Charlottetown the government paid 50 cents per thousand gallons, while at GaspS they paid 50 cents per hundred gallons. Surely there cannot be such a difference in the conditions as to justify a price in one place ten times as high as the other. I believe they can secure fresh water at Gaspe just as cheaply as they can at Charlottetown.
At Charlottetown they have a system of water works, while at Gaspe, I should suppose, they have not. That would make all the difference in the world.

And at another place the government are charged for 700 gallons at the rate of 50 cents per hundred gallons. Again, I find where it is sold by the ton. In one case ten tons at 81-12 a ton, and in another 65 tons at 56 cents per ton-one price exactly double the other, though there seems to be no difference in the conditions. It is manifest that there is something wrong with the system. I do not want to charge any one with giving an erroneous certificate. But there is so much in the Auditor General's Report that is not susceptible of explanation by the ordinary reader that I think the matter is worthy the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries ; and, as he is starting out fresh in the business, I hope that he will make such changes that when we discuss the matter of supplies again, we shall not have to criticise his department in the way which it has been criticised to-night.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understood the hon. minister of Marine and Fisheries, in spite of what has been said, to announce that he intends to continue the present system. When this government came into office, it was loudly proclaimed as a business government, one that would carry on public affairs on business principles. Is the hon. gentleman acquainted with the Ontario and Richelieu Navigation Company ? I am sure he is, for the bead-quarters of that company a^e in the city to which he belongs. They have a fleet of steamers, just as the hon. minister is entrusted with the fleet of steamers for the people of Canada. Will he copy the business methods of that company ?
If they are good.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
That company furnish passenger steamers altogether, and they know the average price of every staple article supplied to those steamers.
Do they go to retail merchants in the various cities for their supplies ? No ; they receive tenders from wholesale houses and they buy the supplies wholesale and distribute them among their steamers. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries lias eight or ten steamers requiring large quantities of staple supplies. Yet, he buys from the retail man at exorbitant retail prices. One hon. gentleman referred to Scott, of Halifax. He said that was a reputable firm and would not overcharge. Let me give him a few articles. Rice, 25 pounds at seven cents per pound.
Where is that ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Auditor General's Report. Page P-19.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) That is the ordinary price in Halifax.

Oh, oh.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Halifax, N.S.) That is the ordinary price for the best quality.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then we have a charge of 25 pounds of currants at 12 cents. And everybody knows that you can buy three pounds at retail for 25 cents. Then I find at page P-17, Charles F. Francis & Co., St. John, charging for beans at 81.95 per per bushel and peas at 81-95 per bushel. Every farmer in the country knows that 81.95 for peas and beans is an outrageous price. If the government were buying these in a large quantity and delivering them to their several steamers, they could get much lower prices, and the same with all staple articles, such as sugar, rice, flour and so on.
I suppose that the hon. gentleman is aware that last year-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
When I get through, my hon. friend (Mr. Tobin) can answer me or can ask all the questions he likes. Or, if he

wishes to ask me a question now, I have no objection.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that the wholesale price for beans last year was from $1.80 to $2 according to the quality ?

The quantity of peas and the quantity of beans bought In this case was one bushel each.
i Mr. TAYLOR. And the price was $1.95. The hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe (Mr. Tobin) cannot find that these articles were sold at such prices as he states in any market.
I bought them in my own line of business.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Let the hon. gentleman ask the hon. member for Essex who sits near him, and he knows the prices.
Beans were shipped from the county of Kent last season at about $1.75 per bushel. The farmers received from $1.50 to $1.60 per bushel.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Whether the system is right or wrong, I ask the government to do business on business principles, as they promised to do. I ask them to adopt the system followed by the Richelieu Navigation Company, and every other company in Canada having big steamers to supply, and who buy their staple supplies from wholesale firms by tender, or from some friends at wholesale prices. But do not go about the country to these little two penny ha'penny stores and buy at prices two or three times higher than they could buy at home in every part of Canada. There is not one hon. gentleman on the treasury benches who is paying the prices for goods in his own home that are charged here for the supply of these steamers. Every man on the other side of the House must know that some of the prices that are certified to are exorbitant and extravagant prices, that they would not pay for goods of the same kind to be used in their own homes.

I would ask the Minister of Finance one question. Shortly after the government came into power they adopted the system along the St. Lawrence river of calling for tenders for the supply of goods. That system was carried on for a couple of years, when they ceased doing that, and the last five or six years the supplies have been purchased from retail merchants along the line, and certified to, as I understand, by the officer in charge at the place where they are bought with the words * prices fair and just.' But the minister knows that that officer gets his instructions from the department that employs him, he has purchased his goods from a certain retail merchant in that town, and that officer knows well that if he did not certify to the prices as fair and just his head would Mr. TAYLOR.
be cut off within twenty-four hours, because that retail merchant would have him dismissed, there is no doubt about that. The head of the department would not stand that officer criticising the prices. Now why did the Minister of Finance change that system of calling for tenders and go back to the system that'is now being complained of?

I am not aware that such change has taken place as the hon. gentleman alleges. Of course, that is a matter for the Department of Marine and Fisheries to attend to, but I do not think any such change has taken place.
I never said it took place.

He says it has taken place in certain contracts, but my impression is that he is mistaken. As to the other point about the local officials, his statement is a very remarkable one ; I hope it would not have been true under the late government, I know it is not true under the present government. He stated that an official is obliged to certify to fraudulent accounts otherwise he would be dismissed. My hon. friend treats that as a light matter. He speaks as if he would have considered that the regular method under the old government. I trust that it was not done under the late government, 1 do not believe it was ; I know it is not done under the present government. I am sure that any officer who would report to the head of the department that the prices were too high and ought to be reduced, would be commended, as he ought to be, for the performance of his duty. But the suggestion that an official of this department, or of any other department, is obliged to certify to accounts which are not fair and just, is a very unfair one, and I am sure the hon. gentleman, on reflection, will not justify it. I know it is not justified with regard to these officials to whom I have referred, and who were appointed by the late government. I have only to say that if they were asked to give such certificates of prices being fair and reasonable when they knew they were not, they are manly enough to throw up their places at once rather than hold them on such a condition.

I would like to say to the Minister of Finance that under the late government that system was ngt required by the Auditor General until shortly before we ceased holding office, and it was on account of prices at different points being higher than he supposed they ought to be that he insisted on those words being put on the invoices. Now I know for a fact that officials who are in charge of certain works do and have certified to accounts such as I have mentioned, and I know well enough that if they did not certify to the accounts that were handed in, their heads would be cut off, and the ministers at the

beads of the departments know it too. Their officials are told to purchase from certain parties, and I know well that these same officials can purchase goods cheaper from the same parties for their own use. I am not finding fault with the officials, it is their bread and butter to hold their positions.
I do find fault with those officials. An official who will certify that a price is fair and reasonable when he knows that the certificate is false, has no right to be in the public service.

How is the official to know ? Does the Minister of Finance mean to say that if he has complaints made to him against this official for objecting to the accounts he would not be hauled over the coals and dismissed ?
He would be dismissed if he did not object.

The hon. gentleman asks how the official is to know. He stated just now that the official bought goods for himself cheaper than he bought for the government, and that he certified to an account for goods bought at a higher price for the government.

The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) stated in the fore part of the evening that certain lots of hardware had been purchased, and that ail the way from 20, 25 and 30 to 40 percent had been paid over and above the market value. I thought that was rather an extravagant statement, and my curiosity iuduced me to refer to the Auditor General's Report, and I find that the statement made by my hon. friend is well within the mark. On page P-9, I find there are 8,780 pounds of ordinary iron charged at three cents a pound. Now that iron at the time it was supplied to the government could be sold in those quantities by any wholesale hardware man for $1.95, or by any extensive retailer for about $2.10 or $2.25. That was sold at Quebec, and the prices I am- giving you are the prices at which you can buy it at Ottawa.
What is the name of the Quebec dealer ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Drolet. I also find an item for 994 pounds of zinc, equal to about two casks, and that zinc is charged at the rate of 15 cents a pound. When this was purchased, zinc by casks, was selling at GJ cents. I am speaking of something about which I know. To-day, zinc is higher than it has been for the last three years, and it is selling at 7 cents. If you buy it from a Tory you can get it for 7 cents. Iron is dearer than it has been for the last three years, but you could buy iron for $2.25 per hundred pounds in any retail store in Ottawa. I will sell you all you want for $2
per hundred. I find that the government paid 3 cents a pound. Another item is 93 pounds of Magnolia metal at 40 cents a pound. There is only one quality of Magnolia metal made and you can get any quantity you want of it for 224 cents a pound. Another item is machine steel of which 761 pounds were purchased at 6 cents a pound. That is retail. I cannot give the size because the size is not given here, but the standard size which is f inch is selling in any retail store for $3 per hundred. I could go through the list and point out many similar charges. I think I have shown sufficient to convince this committee that when the government are spending public money, supplies ought to be furnished by public competition. I do not go so far as some hon. members here who say that probably the heads of departments when certifying to these accounts as being fair and just do it without the information. Probably they may have done it without the information, but we have to bear in mind that their information is limited to the extent of these circulars. I suppose the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries will tell me that it is a machinist company which supplied these goods. I admit it is a machinist company that supplied these goods, but these are the prices that it has charged for the goods themselves. There has been no work put upon these goods because 2,369 hours of work is charged for at the rate of 35 cents an hour. The prices which I have quoted are the actual prices paid for these goods, and I have also given the prices which these goods ought to have cost if they had been purchased in any store in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I knew that I was not far from the mark when I stated at the beginning of this debate that if some system of tendering were adopted- I am not accusing any one department more than another-we could save at least from 25 to 30 per cent. I passed through the mill. I changed the system in the Department of Public Works. We were buying in that department right and left, just as the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries is buying now. We opened a store in Ottawa and we have saved between 30 and 40 percent since that store has been opened. It is true it is not perfect, but since we have had that system we have, I repeat, saved between 30 and 40 per cent The hon. minister is just taking hold of his department, and I would suggest to him to adopt the same system. Let him open stores. Let him ask for tenders, even if he does not ask for tenders in the public press, but simply asks for tenders from wholesale merchants as big companies do. I am not inclined to go so far as some hon. gentlemen here who say that every time the government must ask for public tenders. If we follow the rule of asking for tenders from wholesale merchants we will save from 25 to 30 ner cent

every time. But, I insist specialty on this point, and I give this suggestion in no unfriendly spirit, that the hon. gentleman should open stores and let the officers from the different ships draw from those stores. If he does he will control the expenditure which is not controlled now. Before taking my seat let me say that I do not share the views of those hon. gentlemen who say that officers in the public service must not have some little luxuries. I went into that question when I was Minister of Public Works. Take the case of the commander and officers of the ships of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. They spend seven or eight months of the year on the water. They must have some little luxuries. When a case came before me I went to the Canadian Pacific Railway, president and managers, and asked them what their rule was. They told me that their rule was to give their officers mineral waters, Apollinards and so on. Cigarettes, of course, is going a little too far. Mineral waters and things of that kind, I think, should be allowed to public officers in cases such as we have been discussing. This country has no necessity to be mean. We are a very big country and we are growing bigger every day. Let us treat our officers as we deal with ourselves. They are gentlemen. Let us not allow them to make useless expenditures, but let us not go too far the other way. If the hon. minister takes the suggestions which have been made in the proper spirit, I think he will derive some benefit from what has been said. There is no doubt whatever that from 25 to SO per cent can be saved from the adoption of the plan which I have suggested. That system was adopted by my own department a year or two ago, and I found it not only very economical but more comfortable.

Has the hon. minister submitted to the committee, or has he under his hand, a statement showing the cost per man per day on each of the government steamers for rations and pay ? There should be such a statement prepared regularly and it should be submitted to the House.
It cost 33 cents and a fraction per man per day.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I would like to say to the hon. Minister of Finance again in connection with the system of calling for tenders that shortly after the Liberal government came into power they advertised for tenders for supplies for the St. Lawrence canals. They did not say how much of each article they required but they gave a list of supplies that would be required.
We are discussing Marine and Fisheries now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
That may be, but I am pointing out that the system has been Hon. Mr. TARTE.
changed in connection with the St. Lawrence canals.
The system of the Marine and Fisheries Department is the one we are talking about now.
Before that they purchased their supplies the same way.

They are not under discussion at all.
Mr. REID (Grenville), It is the same principle. The hon. minister states that there is no officer of the government who would certify to prices unless he thought they were fair and just. Take an instance of that kind. I want to refer to it although it is not in the Marine Department. On the St. Lawrence canals, tenderers were advertised for, and the officer had that tender to guide him that the price was fair and just, but that system has been abolished by this government. You will find now that at Cardinal, Mr. Stewart, the superintendent will pay 21 cents for coal oil, and five miles east he will pay 18 cents while if he bought it at Iroquois for 18 cents he could take it down to Cardinal at no cost whatever. The officer is told to purchase from certain parties in each town, and if the officer does not certify to the accounts he would not hold his position for forty-eight hours.
My hon. friend's conception of Liberal government is entirely erroneous.
The facts prove I am right.

The facts do not prove it. The hon. gentleman says that if that officer did not certify to what is practically a fraudulent account he would lose his office. He has no warrant for that. If he could show any instance where an officer has lost his head because of that he would have good ground to go on. I suppose the hon. gentleman did not intend it as such, but it is a reflection upon every officer in Canada who certifies to these accounts, and it implies that these officers are forced by this government to certify fraudulent accounts. The hon. gentleman would not go so far as that, but that is a fair deduction from what he says.
Mr. REID (Grenville), I did not say they certified to fraudulent accounts, but they certainly have to accept the accounts of the parties who furnish them and the officer takes the word of the seller for it.
If an officer certifies to an account as fair and reasonable the certificate is true or it is not true.
Regardless of whether they are fair or not ?
How does he know ?
It is his business to know.

The officer has no choice in the matter. The hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) *who is a hardware merchant tells us that fifteen cents a pound is twice too much for zinc, and if you go through all these estimates, you will find that the government is paying from 100 to 150 per cent more for these supplies than they could be purchased for in the ordinary retail way, and these accounts are certified to by the officer who is forced to go there by the Liberal member who represents that constituency. The member for Kent (Mr. Stephens) will be able to tell us that my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett), is quite correct in what he says.

The hon. member from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) quoted the price of iron and he says this iron was supplied by a machinist. To my mind part of the work done on this machine steel and iron was done in the factory and charged with the price of the iron, which Is the common way of doing it in machine shops. The smaller the iron the more it counts, and the price he has quoted may have been for a smaller size of iron.
Are the prices I gave on standard goods correct ?
We do not know whether this iron is common iron or whether it is Swede or Norway iron.
We cannot buy Swede at any such price, and we know that the Quebec merchants are not in the habit of selling goods at much less than cost.
We do not know whether it is angle iron or round.
That would not make any difference.
As a rule angle iron is more expensive than square or round.

There is 761 pounds of machine steel at six cents a pound, and is not that 100 per cent too much ?
Mr, STEPHENS. There may have been workmanship on it and it may not have been too much.
The workmanship is charged extra in every case.
You cannot tell from the statement in the Auditor General's Report whether it is or not.

These accounts are for articles purchased two years ago, some of them, and I do not suppose that we can carry in our heads what the prices were then. The Auditor General's Report is so condensed that you cannot get a proper understanding of such matters from it. I do not remember as much about hardware as when I was a boy serving* in a hard-ware store, but the hoii. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) is familiar with the trade, and he knows that Swede iron is very much more valuable than common iron. Now the Auditor General's Report is very much condensed, and it mav be possible that part of this is Swede iron and part of it common iron. When these accounts were examined two years ago there was a mystery about one of them, and we found it was another article altogether that was charged for it. The hon. member for Leeds the other night in going through the accounts of my department stated that certain prices were outrageous and I promised him that I would inquire into it. There is an officer in the department who has been in the employment for years, and I asked him next morning for an explanation, calling his attention to the remarks that were made. I must say that Mr. Bleakney, the officer in question, gave me a very satisfactory explanation. I asked him how he came to go to that place, as I had not told him to go to any particular place. He said that he had a letter from the private secretary stating that another house was entitled to a share of the patronage ; but he said he had bought very little there, because he could buy the goods cheaper elsewhere. I asked him if he scrutinized every account so carefully. He said most certainly he did. I suppose the other officers do the same. We cannot judge from the condensed report given by the Auditor General. It looks to me, from the price of sugar, as I know it, as if some of these prices might be a little high. 1 cannot carry my mind back to say how the sugar market was two years ago. Sugar fluctuates, and I know that iron and steel have varied very much within a few years.
How many years ?
I do not know, but I know that we had to raise the invoices tremendously.
Oh, no.

Yes, in iron and steel in some cases 50 per cent. So it does not do to make sweeping reductions. I am sure that under the officer's of my de-



partment tlie prices will be found to be | right.

I have no desire to misquote or misrepresent anything I find in the Auditor General's Report. I have given one item of which there is only one quality made, that is, magnolia metal ; and for that 174 cents a pound more is charged than you could buy it at any time in the last three years. There has been no change in that. With regard to iron, two years ago I sold it at $1.95. There has not been any great change in the price of iron or steel.
Oh, yes.

I beg pardon. . I am dealing in it every day. I know that sometimes the government will insist on an amended entry, on information which they get from the ' Iron Age,' which is their only authority. You might as well take the ordinary daily report in our newspapers. You can go to the manufacturers and buy iron at a price, but all you get in the ' Iron Age ' is the current retail price ; but the Customs Department, not only here, but in every other city, swears by that as by the Bible. There is where they make a mistake. So far as iron and steel are concerned, I am perfectly correct in the quotations I have given. The hon. member for Kent says nothing about zinc, which is worth from 4c. to 4c. a pound more to-day than it was last year, and it was still lower the year before. Here the government is charged for it 15 cents a pound, or 100 per cent more than it is selling at to-day, the highest price the market has reached in the last four years. With regard to iron, I gave the base price. Three-quarter inch is the base ; each one-sixteenth-inch less is 5 cents per hundred weight more until you reach three-sixteenth inch, so that even if it was the smallest iron that was produced, the price is extravagant. The hon. member for Kent said that probably this was Swede iron. These people in Quebec are not such fools as to send invoices for 5,800 pounds of iron, and not mention that it was Swedish iron if it was so. The accounts are prepared in such a way as to make the best show, and if it were put at a price basis to correspond with that of common iron, it would cost five or six cents a pound. The price'charged for steel is also 100 per cent more than it could be bought at if it was standard size. Wrlien I first mentioned the matter, I told you what size the iron or steel was ; but presuming that it was base size, the price of the iron is $1.05 more than should be charged for it, and for base steel 3 cents per pound, or 100 per cent more than ought to be charged for it.
I have given attention to the hon. gentleman's statement, because I know that he is engaged in the iron trade ; but what he has said has shaken my confidence.
I cannot help that.

When he says that there has been no variation in the price of iron and steel for five or six years,
I cannot agree with him. I know that within a much less period than that we have raised the invoices from 25 per cent to 50 per cent, and I am not sure but 100 per cent. The hon. gentleman must know how steel and iron went up in price.
The hon. gentleman is completely in error. Three years ago iron was cheaper than it is to-day.

The hon. gentleman is bringing it down to three years now. I was perfectly sure in what I said, going back, as he said, six or eight years.
I thought the rise would perhaps be within three years ; but I will make a point of looking it up and ascertaining when we had to call for these amended entries. There were many contracts given for future delivery, eight or ten months afterwards, and during that time the price went up 50 per cent, and in some cases more.

I said that if the hon. gentleman would go back three years he would find that iron was cheaper three years ago than it is to-day. Iron is a thing that fluctuates. But when hon. gentlemen talk of twenty, fifty and in some cases one hundred per cent increase, no such change has taken place since the big change took place when fifty cents per hundred pounds was put on in 1878. Iron then went up very rapidly because it was nearly all imported, but I am quite positive that three years ago we sold iron at $1.85 and two years ago at $1,924, and last year at $1.95. I am quite within the mark when I say three years. The hon. Minister of Customs says that there is a price quoted in ' Iron Age.' If the customs officer says that black is white, the burden is on the importer, of proving that it is not. The customs officer says, we cannot accept that, and the importer has to prove why it should be accepted.

The hon. Minister of Customs has said that he is not well versed in the price of iron as he is in some other matters. He ought to be fairly well versed in the price of sugar, and if he will go back two years, that will not make the matter any better with regard to the quotation given by the hon. member for Hal-ton. Two years ago standard granulated sugar was lower than during the past year. Take another item in which the hon. minister should be well versed-the item of biscuits-the pilot or water biscuits are charged at different prices, from six to eight cents a pound. The hon. gentleman should have some idea whether that is a fair price. Mixed biscuits are charged at seventeen to eighteen cents per pound. It must be a pretty fine article at that price. I

did not look over tlie Auditor General's Report until this evening, and I find that there are columns of items at from twenty-five to thirty per cent higher than they could be got for by tender. We have been assured by the Minister of Finance that because these accounts were certified to by officials as reasonable and fair we should accept them, but evidently what would be reasonable and fair in any other business transaction does not apply to government supply. It is quite evident that these men know what they are certifying to, and that this debate has brought out the assurance that the contract would be given to friends of the government. I do not know whether this will be satisfactory to the country, but lam Inclined to think that it will not.

Having had some thirty years experience in the business of tea and coffee, perhaps my silence would be taken as endorsing the criticism of the opposition. It seems to me most unfair that hon. gentlemen should attempt to criticise the purchases of these supplies by taking items out of the Auditor General's Report without knowing the quality of the goods. Take the item of tea. We have in our store at present, tea which we sell at ten cents, and also tea which we sell at fifty cents, and it is most unfair to criticise the price of tea without knowing the quality. The hon. member for St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte) said that the very best quality of coffee can be bought in Montreal at thirty cents a pound. I do not wish to contradict my hon. friend, but if his statement is correct. you can buy coffee cheaper at retail in Montreal than at wholesale. We have a coffee which we purchase at Montreal and which costs us thirty-two cents per pound at -wholesale. I am positive that they do not retail that coffee at thirty cents.
The next time I come up I will send a pound to my hon. friend.
I do not wish to be understood as not believing what my hon. friend has said, but if he pays thirty cents he does not buy the very best coffee.
It is the very best quality and I know what coffee is.

There is the matter of baking powder, which can be bought at $2 to SO per dozen. How can hon. gentlemen opposite look at the price of that and judge as to the quality. As regards sugar, that is now in the hands of a combine, and whenever there is a change in price, a telegram is sent and the change must take place immediately. When a telegram is sent from the refinery every wholesale merchant must raise and lower his prices at once. The price of beans, $1.60 and $1.95 has been referred to. As a wholesale merchant I know that beans at $1.60 and $1.95 or even $2, anv time within 129J
a year and a half, is a very low price lower than they have been sold at in the western part of the maritime provinces at retail. With reference to currants at twelve cents per pound, there is a difference between ordinary currants and those put up in one pound packages. Personally I have had some little experience in supplying goods to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Unfortunately I never had a chance of supplying very many goods, but when I did supply any, I never met sharper men than the shipmasters of the government, and it would be almost impossible for anybody to overcharge them. The hon. member for Northumberland thought that the captain and the crews of those boats were too well treated. If he had had the experience with captains that I have had, he would find that the best quality of goods is none too good for people that go to sea, and I do not blame them for getting the very best. Under all the circumstances, I do not see anything in the grocery list that shows any over charge.

I would nice to make a few remarks with regard to this account of F. X. Drolet. The hon. member for Kent, in his defence of the charges in. this account, particularly in connection with the charge for steel and iron, stated that he could not give an answer to the question put to him because there might have been a certain amount of work put on this steel. Turning to page P-9 of the Auditor General's Report I find that that account reads ' repairing steam engine, making shaft, screw condenser keel "and steam connections to boiler, $250.' Going further down you will find time charged up by these parties : 387i hours at 50 cents ; 1,3364 hours at 40 cents ; 2,369 hours at 35 cents ; 4,909 hours at 30 cents ; 1,7174 hours at 25 cents ; 2,757 hours at 20 cents ; 160 hours at 15 cents. .Now, I think there was sufficient time charged to make all repairs necessary, and there is no doubt that this six cents was charged for steel. No amount of sophistry by the hon. Minister of Customs will get over that. Machinery steel, two years ago was not more than $2.75 retail. That would buy the best quality of hard machinery steel. Here we are buying almost half a ton at $6 per 100 pounds. Then zinc, which can be purchased in casks at from five to six cents is charged at fifteen cents. There are large qualities of zinc charged elsewhere at the same money. The hon. member for Kent (Mr. Stephens) knows that the magnolia is a standard article and retails everywhere at 224 cents, yet 40 cents is charged. Talk of ten, fifteen and twenty per cent advances, they are not in it with this. There is anywhere from 100 to 150 per cent overcharge here in hardware. I believe it would be in the interest of the department and the country if the minister would call for tenders for these articles rather than continue buying by this system.

Rut. i! a job is sent to a mechanic's shop, can you first get tenders for the materials, buy them at competitive prices and send them to the mechanic and oblige him to use them? If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Thomson, Grey) sends for the plumber to do work in his house ; will that plumber charge the hon. gentleman for materials at wholesale prices? Surely, the charge will include a profit. So, when you send work to a mechanic's establishment you must expect him to charge for material with a profit. It should be a fair and reasonable profit of course.
I submit that the answer of the Minister of Finance is not satisfactory.
I hardly expected the hon. member (Mr. Thompson) to be satisfied.

It will not be
satisfactory to the country. Here we find an article that when bought in small quantities sells at six cents, charged at fifteen cents per pound, though about half a ton was bought. At page P-32 of the Auditor General's Report, I find 225 pounds of zinc charged at 15 cents per pound, though it can be bought in quantities at five cents per pound and retail at six cents per pound. Now. these are facts, and it is for hon. members of the committee to take note of them and judge whether a system which leads to such charges is a good system or not.

There is no doubt in my mind that the explanation of these charges is that work was done on material furnished for repairs. As to magnolia, the hon. gentleman says that only one quality of magnolia is made. I believe that, as a rule, thnt is the case. But the hon. gentleman knows that they could make magnolia worth a good deal more money and It is likely that a special order was given for magnolia for this purpose. Hon. gentlemen talk about coal oil, which is bought at one place for 21 cents and another place for 19 cents. Hon. gentlemen know that coal oil fluctuates from one season to the other. _Ameri-can coal oil would probably cost 25 cents, while Canadian oil would be cheap at 20 cents. Then, take the case of iron pipe. I have no doubt that this is cut into lengths The iron bolts would be cut into lengths and turned in the lathes. The pipe, no doubt, was cut into lengths and threaded for the purpose of making railings and so on. This would explain the cost.
We find 16 feet of one inch pipe charged. Does the hon. gentleman say that that is cut in lengths and the charge made in this way ?
It might be.

What reasons has the hon. gentleman to believe that ?
Mr. THOMSON INorth Grey).
Because, in building a boat they would not use one length of pipe 16 feet. It is used in short lengths for railings, and so on. It would probably be cut into lengths, threaded and coupled up.

What is there in the item to lead the hon. gentleman to suppose that these charges include work ? When hon. gentlemen opposite were on this side they took a different view of the Auditor General's Report. The Minister of Customs did not take the same view that he takes tonight.
You had it put then so that you could understand it.
The item shows plainly that too much has been charged.

The illustration of the plumber given by the Minister of Finance is a. fair one. But it does not apply altogether to this case. If you employ a plumber, he is supposed to buy his material at first hand, he Charges you the retail price. If that was all in this case, we should be quite satisfied. The hon. gentleman knows that the plumbers bill always comes in-so many pounds of pipe, so many pounds of solder, and so many pounds of everything else-even putty-and then so many hours of time. I am perfectly satisfied that the Minister of Finance in drawing his comparison with the plumbers' bill was perfectly honest. And it is quite fair to say that these contractors are entitled to retail prices for these goods. But, they are away in excess in their charges for iron and steel.

I notice an item here of 28 pounds of solder at 40 cents a pound. The regular price of solder is 25 cents, as almost any gentleman in the House is aware. Here are two hammocks bought from M . C. Blakiston, Quebec, at $5 a piece. Page P- 21 of the Auditor General's Report. I find varnish, 17i gallons at $6 per gallon; 2 wheelbarrows at $7 a piece. There are several items here that I am perfectly convinced are at least 50 per cent and in some cases $100 per cent higher than they could be supplied to the government under contract. Now there is an important principle involved. The Liberal-Conservative party say that these goods should be supplied to the government by tender, the government say, no, these goods shall not be supplied by tender, and the minister now says that notwithstanding the criticisms that has been offered he will continue in that policy, and will refuse to ask for tenders for goods to be supplied to the government. I wish to remind the hon. gentleman that in the province of Ontario, from which I come, every municipal council gets its supplies by tender. If they want the minutes of council printed, though the expense is only $50 or $G0, if they want to make a purchase of nails or supplies for the corporation, they ask for

tenders. There is hardly any corporation who is purchasing supplies, no matter how small a quantity, but ask for tenders. When the Liberal-Conservative party were in power the hon. gentlemen opposite criticised the former government for not buying everything by tender. I do not say it is possible for the government in every case to buy every dollar's worth of goods by tender. But here is a line of steamers which are supplied with goods of the same class every year; they require so many pounds of sugar, so much varnish, so niuch iron-the same class of goods every year, the boats plying between the same places year after year. The minister knows very well that he will require the same goods every year, and I think it is only fair to the people of this country, when he is asking us for $250,000, on which only $15,000 revenue is returned, that he Should ask for tenders for the supply of these vessels. If there are some goods that cannot be bought by tender, I am willing he should buy them from his friends. That is fair play and the Liberal-Conservative party well understand it. For myself, I object to this large expenditure and the very high i>rices, extortionate prices in some cases, that have been charged during the last year. I say it is fair to the people and it is fair to this committee that the minister should now stand up and say that in future these large supplies shall be bought by public tender.

I think a good many of the criticisms made by hon. gentlemen opposite about the Marine Department are made under a misconception. So far as I understand it, the Marine Department, in all the leading articles it requires, has been in the habit of asking for tenders every year. But the debate has been going on under a different impression entirely. It is asserted that no tenders have been called for, and the kind advice is given to the new minister to call for tenders. If he has been doing that in the past and is doing it now, that advice is gratuitous. What if a few small potatoes for the crew, and a few scraps of iron for the use of the steamer are purchased without tender ? The officers must purchase these small things in the ports where they stop.
There was one item of over $0,000.

For a number of articles included in that item, I think you will find probably that the minister called for tenders, he takes an offer from the person who is doing the repairs. I think that has been the practice of the department in the past. Now this debate has taken a wide range, and I wish to reply to some of the reflections that have been made on some of the dealers in Prince Edward Island. Some hon. members have referred to them as charging unduly high prices. I think you will find in Charlottetown as fair dealing
men as you will find anywhere else in Canada. They have mentioned bananas, and pease and beans, which I am sorry to say we have to bring down from Ontario. Articles like these may be charged a little higher price because they have to pay freight on them. For bananas and fruit, of course, the price is higher there because they have to be imported in small quantities. Reflections are made upon the Marine Department and upon the minister for paying too high prices. The agent of the Department of Marine in Prince Edward Island, Mr. Lord, 'has been there for a great many years. He has been employed under the Conservative administration, and is a most careful man. I do not think he would certify to any prices as fair and reasonable unless he really believed they were so. Many of the prices charged in Prince Edward Island are very moderate, they are not nearly equal to the prices charged in other places in Canada. A reflection has also been made on the officials in charge of the steamers because it is alleged some of them use cigarettes. or some of them did not do their duty in managing the steamers during the winter. I have not taken the trouble to speak on this subject, because if there is one thing more than another I dislike it is airing grievances, when those grievances are of a very flimsy character. Captain Brown has been specially named, the captain of the ' Stanley.' I know that there is no more capable, no more honourable and conscientious captain sailing across the Atlantic ocean to-day. There is not a man of any standing in Prince Edward Island who would reflect upon his character. Captain Finlayson of the ' Minto' has been for twenty or thirty years conducting the service aci-oss the straits, as captain of that boat. He is a capable, economical and faithful officer. Both of these men are exceedingly capable and prudent. I am sorry to hear reflections cast upon them and especially by hon. members from our own province, because these reflections that are cast upon these men should be directed towards those who are circulating stories and rumours against these officers. I must admit that there was a lot of trouble during last winter but it was caused by the fact that there was more ice in the straits of Northumberland separating the island from the mainland than there had been for twenty or twenty-five years past. We should not undertake to abuse these officers simply because nature was against us last winter. We were unfortunate in our effort to conduct this service simply because of the ice. There were three miles of ice around the ' Stanley ' and she was kept there month after month. It is a matter that we are all seeking to remedy, but there is no remedy in abusing the officers who are connected with the Department of Marine and Fisheries. We have capable men in the service and I think it is wrong to reflect upon them.
Are the quotations right that we have been giving you ?

I do not hear the hon. gentleman. I think we can remedy the difficulties down there and we have some plans by which we hope to provide a remedy. I am sorry to hear hon. gentlemen casting reflections upon our province. Its relation to Canada is the same as the relation of the eye to the body. If you injure the eye you injure the body. Prince Edward Island is a small part of Canada, and if you reflect upon Prince Edward Island and the business men of Prince Edward Island, you reflect upon Canada.
Who did it V

I would not have made these remarks at all but for the attacks made upon the officers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, who are good men, some of them Conservatives, and all men who have had a long experience.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclcinnon) who has just taken his seat, seems to find fault with this side of the House because we are criticising the extravagance of this government. I claim that this government has been extravagant in many ways and particularly because they have not adopted the practice of inviting tenders for supplies. There is no use in finding fault with us because we condemn such extravagance. We are here to represent the wishes of the people, and if the people are not satisfied with being robbed in this way it is our duty to protest against the system. I find, for instance, that beans have been purchased at from $2 to $2.25 a bushel, when we all know that beans have never been worth that. If they are to be purchased at that price, why not give the people throughout the country a chance to put in tenders for such supplies as these. It has always been customary to do that when furnishing supplies to county councils, cities and towns, and why should not the government carry out the same system ? The hon. member for Kent (Mr. Stephens) says that iron and machinery have been bought and work added to them. That is not the case, because I have been purchasing non and machinery in machine shops, and the rule is that they charge so much for the iron and they charge for the number of hours work that they put upon them.
Would the hon. member (Mr. Avery) say that iron is never partly worked up and not charged for ?
No, it is not customary for any machine shop to put work upon iron without charging for it.
Does the hon. gentleman say it is never done ?

It has never been done in my case. They charge for the number of pounds of iron purchased and they charge for the number of hours labour they put upon it, either round iron, or square iron as well as the metal they run. The hon. gentleman is only making a statement that he thinks to be so, but he has no proof. I have proof that they charge for the iron in its raw state and they charge for the work afterwards. I think it would help the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries considerably if he would adopt the plan of asking for tenders. It would relieve him of a lot of trouble.

The hon. gentleman is under an entire misapprehension. I said that tenders were asked for standard goods when a certain quantity was required at a certain point, but that there were articles for which we could not ask for tenders.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Would the hou. minister say that lie would ask for tenders from this out for whatever staple goods he required 7

I have always done it. It has been the custom of the department for years. I found the custom of the department to be that, and I proceeded in the same way this season when the time came to put the steamers into commission. I did that in Quebec. I had twenty tenders for groceries alone.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Did the hon. minister advertise or send out circulars ?
I sent out circulars.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Would it not be better to advertise and give the merchants of the country a chance to tender ?
The MINISTER	OF	MARINE	ANDFISHERIES. That	is a	question	of calculation. In a place where you wanted $200 worth of goods would you pay a newspaper $100, or $150, or $200 for advertising ? If you think that is good policy I do not think it is.

Would the hon. minister inform the committee if he asked for tenders for zinc ?
The MINISTER	OF	MARINE	ANDFISHERIES. The	hon.	gentleman	(Mr. Richardson) is not serious when he asks that ? Zinc and magnolia belong to a class of articles that are entirely different from staple goods. You could never ask for tenders for them. I would like the hon. gentleman to tell me how tenders could be asked for them ? Could you say iu advance that this vessal will require $500, or that vessel will require $300, or another vessel will require $100 worth of repairs to be made, and ask for tenders for these repairs?
It is impossible. No business man would do it in that way.
There is no business man who would pay fifteen cents a pound for zinc.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Are we to understand from the hon. minister that he has advertised for all the staple supplies he requires for all the steamers ?
I have not advertised. I have sent circulars to the trade.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
All the supplies for these government steamers, the flour, the sugar, and the coffee, ought to be purchased in bulk and divided between the different steamers.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Of course, that is what I did for the standard articles that we are in need of at every moment.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
What ports ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Quebec, Halifax, St. John, Montreal, Victoria.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Will the minister bring down the tenders he has asked for and the replies ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Certainly.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister says he has adopted this rule of advertising for tenders for all the standard staples, and he will bring down the tenders he received.
At the different ports ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The statement I made last night with reference to the customs accounts rendered by Charleson was that nail pullers were bought at $1.50 each and locks at $125 a gross, and I said that I bought as good a nail puller as could be bought for our factory for $1. He says these locks are sent out to the ports, but he can get one of them back, and let him produce it and lay it on the Table, and I will venture the statement that any hardware man will declare that it is an outrageous price for it.
Bring it up in the Public Accounts Committee.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I will
How much was expended on supplies for these boats last year ?
$35,000 for provisions.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Out of that $35,000 how much was supplied by tender ?
Everything.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Everything ?
Except a few items, may be. If a boat put into port and wanted fresh butter or potatoes, we would not ask for tenders and wait eight days to get the tenders in.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The minister takes issue with this side of the House, and answers our criticisms by saying that he has already adopted that policy.
Of course.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Now, what amount of this $35,000 was supplied under tender ?
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND 1'iSHERIES. Nobody could carry all the details of these small items in his head, but I will get them. I will lay the statement on the Table of the House with the schedules.
Would not this be a good time to have them ?
If the minister says he will bring it down, it is all right.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Was there a tender for sugar at the port of Halifax last year ?
I am informed by the deputy that there was.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The lowest tender would be accepted for the supply of all the sugar at that port ?
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Did the minister receive a tender from Charles A. Parent, of Quebec ? At page P-12 of the Auditor General's Report I find the following charges made by him : 31 pounds of flax packing at 90 cents a pound, which should have cost about 35 cents ; 14 gallons of gasolene at 75 cents a gallon, which every hardware man knows retails at 35 cents ; 5 gallons of lavender paint at $2.50 a gallon, which costs from $1 to $1.10 a gallon. Probably the member for Kent (Mr. Stephens) can tell us whether this is perfumed or not.
That paint costs $1.40.

There is a charge for 15 gallons of terra cotta paint at $2.50 a gallon, which should cost the same as the light lavender, namely, from $1 to $1.10 a gallon. I find in this account also 891 pounds of zinc at 15 cents a pound.
That seems to be the current price.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Yes, they seem to have a fixed price for this department. -But I may inform the hon. minis-

ter that that gentleman had a profit of about $80 on that one item. If that is the case, you should have a different purchasing agent from the one you had last year. I could give you almost any item in connection with the purchase of supplies in the hardware line for that department, and show that it stands in about the same proportion. Prices are in most cases 100 per cent above the retail price. I think it would be well to have some change made in the system of purchasing these supplies. I would like to ask the bon. minister if tenders were asked?

Certainly, tenders were asked, and the accounts in Quebec are examined and passed by the agent there, Mr. Gregory, an employee of the department for the last forty years. If you put his honesty and capacity in doubt, it is a matter that will have to be looked into in the regular way, in the Public Accounts Committee. I would not take the accounts of the Auditor General. They are not the true accounts as rendered by the department. They are grouped in such a manner that they do not show the real price of the goods.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I have an account of another department, and the reason I refer to it is that the hon. minister says the Auditor General's Report is not correct.
I do not say it is not correct. I say it is not properly compiled.
In this account of another department the prices charged are very much the same as those we have been referring to.

We do not undertake to say that the Auditor General's accounts are not correct; but we say that the method of grouping a number of accounts together does not enable lion, gentlemen to form a fair opinion of the prices without knowing the quality of the article and the circumstances under which the goods are supplied. We had just such general charges made a year ago, as we had made to-night, and in every ease when the matter was looked into, it was found that there was a satisfactory explanation, and I have no doubt it will be so in this case.

I must say that I do not think the way in which tile Minister of Finance has put the matter just now is quite fair to the criticism that has been offered from this side of the House. I can instance the case of sugar, in which there was no possible contention that the price was fair and reasonable, or that there were any conditions which should cause an increased price to be paid. Granulated sugar ought to be cheaper in the city of Quebec than in western Ontario ; yet I know of my Mr. THOMSON (North Grey).
own knowledge that twelve months ago standard granulated sugar was sold in western Ontario, inland, where railway as well as water freight had to be paid, at four cents a pound, when the government was charged five cents and five and a half cents a pound at Quebec. The conditions were altogether in favour of the government purchasing as compared with others ; and yet they were charged from 25 to 30 per cent more than a single barrel of sugar was sold for to the farmers in the country. I think the suggestion that has come from this side of the House ought to be adopted, that all these supplies ought to be purchased by public tender-not by circular but by public notice, so that every one would have an opportunity of tendering ; and if in any instance two tenders were the same, let the government certainly give the patronage to their own friends.

I think the Minister of Finance, who desired to hear of any items, in respect to which criticism might be made, ought to be pretty well satisfied with some of those mentioned to-night, about which there seems to be no question on the one side or the other, on the part of gentlemen familiar with the prices. For instance, I have not heard any one claim that 15 cents is a fair price for zinc, and it cannot be said that that is a material on which any work was done. If there are any special conditions which affect the price of these articles, then in justice to the vendors themselves, the information ought to be brought down by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and furnished to the House at a later date. As to some of these items, we cannot have the slightest doubt that the price is very high. I do not know that you can attach much blame to these men, if the government are willing to pay the prices ; they will put them pretty high if they can pass the officers. I do not say, in the absence of proof, that there is any wrong doing ; but there is certainly material calling for some explanation. I do not ask that the item should stand; but I ask that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries shall bring down an explanation of these prices, if there is any.

I am unable to agree with my bon. friend. The mere quoting of these prices from the Auditor General's Report, without any reference to the circumstances under which the goods were supplied, does not give us an intelligent view of the situation. I state that because that has been our experience in the past. Similar cases were brought before the House last year, they were looked into, the explanation was given, and the prices were found to be fair and reasonable; and I have no doubt, speaking generally, that if these prices were inquired into, they would be found to be in the main fair and reasonable. I would suggest to my bon. friend to take two or three of these items

and let us investigate them before the Committee of Public Accounts, and if it can be shown that the prices are excessive we have the same interest as my hon. friend in seeing that we are not imposed upon, and will join them very cordially in putting an end to any fraudulent practices.
Will the hon. gentleman make standard granulated sugar one of the items.

Even in the ease of sugar, I would prefer to know the circumstances under which the goods were ordered. I can imagine that if an order were given down in one of those ports to supply a certain quantity of goods and deliver them on board the ship, it might make a difference. I decline to form a judgment without the information.

Where you find a standard price of between five or six cents per pound, and the article charged at from twelve to sixteen cents per pound. I think that before we go to the Committee on Public Accounts, we should get an explanation from the department of the special conditions which warranted our paying such a price. Why cannot the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries see his officers and give an explanation to-morrow.

I have no doubt that in any case to which the attention of my hon. colleague is drawn, he will do his best to see that he is not imposed upon. I should think that my hon. friend's would desire to have an investigation, and if it be shown that any of these officials have certified that prices were fair and reasonable when they were not, it is high time that we made some change.
I understood from the hon. gentleman from Yarmouth that it was the captains of the vesels who made the purchases ?
In some eases.

I was rather surprised, but so understood him, and he spoke of the particular shrewdness of these men in making the purchases. As regards any one of these officials certifying to the fairness of the prices of all these supplies, it would be utterly impossible for one man to certify to the value of everything required on board a ship. He might be a good judge of groceries and know nothing about hardware. I would not accuse a man of making a false statement even if he did make a mistake, as it would be utterly Impossible for him to be an expert in every article. No doubt he acted in good faith, but perhaps was misled.

I might add with regard to the observations of my hon. friend from Yarmouth, that we can I
quite understand what he means. If goods are ordered at Quebec, they are ordered by the purchasing agent of the government who is there, but if ordered at Yarmouth, where there is no purchasing agent, the captain will buy what he requires and be the judge of the prices.
Some of the purchases we complain of were made at Quebec.
That is what we want to investigate.

I did not say that the captain is to blame nor the agent of the department, but it is the system that is wrong. A recommendation is made by the representative where these supplies are to be purchased, and the captain is compelled to purchase them at the price recommended, and at whatever price the merchant sees fit to charge.

I must take exception to the last part of the hon. gentleman's statement. It may be quite correct that the captain is directed to buy his supplies at a certain place, but it does not follow that he must pay whatever price is asked. He is only bound to buy at a fair and reasonable price.

I understand that the supplies are asked for by means of circulars, but do all the merchants in certain towns get these, or are these circulars sent to only one or two ? In that case, it would be easy for the two merchants to combine and each charge his own price and divide up the order between them.
Tidal service, including the salary of an assistant clerk beyond $400 notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $22,500.
Why this increase of $15,000. ?
That is to provide for the maintenance of the steamer ' Gulnare ' which we require for the tidal service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Why is it necessary to have a steamer ?

The work was not done satisfactorily. Representations were made by the shipping interest and there are reports by Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper and Sir Louis Davies on the subject. I found that the British Admiralty had a boat doing tidal service, which was somewhat too small for ocean work. It was all fitted up for this particular work and could be bought very reasonably-something like $30,WO. The inspector at Halifax reported that the work could not be satisfactorily done without a steamer, and the work was an urgent necessity to the shipping interest.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Would the hou. gentleman say a few words about what the steamer does ?

She is in charge of Mr. Dawson and staff, and takes the current and the soundings in different parts, the facts being made the basis for a chart which is reported to the admiralty office and furnished to those interested in shipping. The work has been heartily endorsed by those interested.
This does not mean that the service will be increased annually by $15,000 ?
No. There is no additional cost except the maintenance of the steamer.
Is that $15,000 a year ?
Yes.
How does the minister explain an increase of $15,000 for the maintenance ?
We have the steamer and we must maintain it. Other steamers cost about $30,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Will the hon. minister give some details ?
There are the wages of the crew, provisions, fuel, and the rest.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What is the crew ?
The salaries will be $2,400, and so on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That is not enough. What are the other items ?
Say fuel, about $3,000, provisions about $2,000-
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That is, if you buy them by circular ?
I do not know how else they could be bought. Then you have ship-chandlery, docking, miscellaneous, making up about $15,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That is a pretty big * miscellaneous.'
Well, you have sliip-chaudlery say $1,000: docking say, $500; coal oil say, $20; miscellaneous say, $1,400. And then there are repairs.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That makes about $10,000 altogether. The hon. minister is only about $5,000 out.

This seems a pretty large sum for the maintenance of a Hon. Mr. PP.EFONTAINE.
thirty thousand dollar steamer. But this is an important work in which Mr. Dawson is engaged, and any reasonable expenditure would be generally approved. But this seems a very considerable amount considering the size of the steamer and the amount for which she was purchased.
I was not present wrhen the item was called. May I ask if this will be a permanent service ?
We cannot promise. It will be maintained as long as the department thinks it useful.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What is to be gained by this service ? What is really the purport of it ?
The best way to explain it is to read what Sir Charles Hibbert Tapper said on the subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I heard that years ago.

I have nothing more. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) had better read it and refresh his memory.
Salaries and expenses of cattle inspection, $3,300.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: There is an increase here of $500.

That is for an inspector at St. John, New Brunswick.
Unforeseen expenses generally, $5,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I was not here for a time, and would like to ask as to the investigation into xvreeks. Fop instance, would the expense of an investigation into such a case as that of the 'Campana' grounding, come out of this item ?
Of course.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Has any investigation taken place in reference to the grounding of the ' Campana ? '
