I am informed that she was got off without damage and no investigation was asked.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: But if the hon. minister would allow me, I think this is a case of pretty large importance. Here is a boat drawing eighteen feet that grounds although the channel has a depth of between thirty-two and thirty-three feet. Evidently there is something wrong.

The Harbour Commissioners in Montreal are perfectly satisfied with the ex-

planation of the pilot. He mistook the light of a barge that was standing at a certain point for the light of the channel and so he went aground. He was out of the channel at the time. The Harbour Commissioners thought it unnecessary to spend money to investigate a fact that was admitted particularly when there was no damage.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I think that this is a case that deserves attention, and I will tell the hon. minister why. There was a steamer anchored in the middle of the channel as the ' Campana ' was coming up. The pilot mistook the light on that steamer for a light on shore, as the hon. minister has said. That is the best evidence that the light on shore is not what it should be. Instead of it being a fixed light it should be a revolving light, that no mistake may be possible. I believe that a small private yacht grounded near the same place for the same reason. So, I believe there is ground for an investigation and for a change in regard to these lights.
We have arranged to provide the lights suggested by the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte). They have not been installed- have not arrived yet. But they will be here within the next thirty days.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Very well.
It is now two o'clock, and I suppose we shall not take up another item at this hour.

My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is willing to reserve any item that any hon. gentleman may wish to have reserved. I hope that my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will agree that we have not made much progress and we might make a little more advance before we retire.
We have been discussing matters of a good deal of importance, and going over the Auditor General's Report. I think we have done enough for to-night.
There are two or three items on which there will be no discussion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman will gain anything by going on. It is now 2 o'clock. Of course, we have just as much endurance as our hon. friends have.
I should think my hon. friend ought to have, because he has not given us the pleasure of company for much of the evening.
Well, I will now.

We might skip the item 175, and pass the other items.
Magnetic Observatory, $2,700 ; meteorological service, $82,803 ; hydrographic surveys, $35,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Where are those stations ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. The magnetic observatory is at a village near Toronto.

Where have the hydrographic surveys been made this year ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. On Lake Winnipeg and Lake Superior, for the present.

Who has charge of those surveys ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Mr. Stewart. The captain is Mr. Zealand, a new appointment, who comes from St. Catharines.
What is the cause of this increase of $850 in the meteorological service ?
It is caused by increases of salaries to different officers on the*survey.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Have you had any maps made of the surveys ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I have not seen any maps of the lakes prepared by the Ottawa government.

AVhile I was in the department, the surveys made under the direction of Mr. Stewart were sent to the Admiralty in England, they were approved of and the letters returning them highly commended the work of the Canadian officers. The maps are printed and distributed, and include the work done by Mr. Stewart up to last fall.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: By whom are they distributed ?
They are sold. They are distributed by the British Admiralty.

I am asking the question because I know that on the lakes nearly all the maps employed are American maps. I have not seen any Canadian maps of the lakes. These maps do not seem to be procurable anywhere. For the trip I took last year I was obliged to buy American maps.
It is to remedy this state of affairs that this department is being organized thoroughly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I am just informed that there are Canadian maps, but I have not seen them.

We will distribute some to the members of the House.
IIou. Mr. TARTE. The American maps are very flue. They are among the best in the world, but if we can do as good work as they do we will not have much to complain of. We have no survey of the harbours and ports on the lakes. In past years the Department of Public Works and the Department of Marine and Fisheries were each of them doing their own work. If the Department of Marine and Fisheries takes over this work there is no objection, I suppose, but I call the hon. minister's attention to this deficiency.

Friday, June 5, 1903.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
